utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number IT-98-32-T, the Prosecutor versus Mitar Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, sir, would you please make the solemn declaration in the card that the usher has handed you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sit down, please. Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Mr. Domazet:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Martinovic, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Martinovic, I shall be asking you questions on behalf of the Defence counsel of Mr. Mitar Vasiljevic. I should like to ask you, before we start, that we make pauses between question and answer. I will do my best to do the same. This will facilitate the work of the interpreters, and also, the French interpretation takes a little longer so would you please wait a few moments before you answer, and you have the screen in front of you which will help you to see when the interpretation has been typed out. Dr. Martinovic, would you begin by introducing yourself to the Court. Give us your particulars; your name, surname, the place and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: I am Primarius Doctor Borisav Martinovic, neuropsychiatrist, therapist, I was born in Zajecar, Serbia, in 1934. And I graduated from the faculty of medicine in Belgrade in 1962, I completed my specialist training in 1970, and since then, I have been a specialist, that is the work that I do today. I have been in the field for 40 years and I am -- I have been a Primarius for 15 years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think that is sufficient.

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: I was also the head of the department, that is to say, the psychiatric department, when the case which is before the Court today occurred.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I was just waiting for the interpretation to be completed. As I said a moment ago, please try and speak slowly so that we get everything in. Thank you. I can see all the particulars relevant to your career. Could you tell me, please, where you are employed at present.

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: I have my own private practice at present. I omitted to say that for 30 years, I have been a forensic expert.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In 1992, where were you and what did you do?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, I was the head of the psychiatric department. We had just separated psychiatry from neurology. That occurred sometime in 1991, and since that time, we opened a purely psychiatric department, a separate department. I was oriented towards what we call social psychiatry which, at that time, was the leading doctrine in the field of psychiatry, generally speaking. I was the department head. I don't know whether you want me to tell you what a department head does, what his job is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I think it would be a good idea if you were to explain to the Court what your duties at that particular time were and, to the best of your recollections, to tell us which doctors worked on the department with you, if you can remember them all and perhaps their names.

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was a long time ago now, but what I can tell you is what the tasks and duties of the department head were. First of all, it is the authorised individual responsible for everything that occurs in the department. Next, he is in charge of work organisation at all levels, that is to say, supervises everything from the cleaning ladies to the head. And then an important function is the education and training of cadres, and Mr. Simic, Dr. Simic, was a case in point. He was a doctor attending specialist training. As a forensic expert, I always insisted on the constant control of medical documents because I always said that one day it could be needed for court purposes, and I think I succeeded in that respect. I instilled this idea and concept into my colleagues. I always said that everything that is written down as a medical document can be, at some point in time, the subject of forensic expertise or be brought up in a case tried in court. Of course, it is the head of the department head as well to implement modern doctrines state-of-the-art doctrine in the field for which he is head, and as this was the initial stage of psychiatry in European psychiatry as well, we always insisted upon this and held seminars and I organised almost 50 seminars in the sphere of modern psychiatry. That, briefly, would be what I did. I think that is enough.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for those explanations. And now, to go back to the second part of my question: As far as you remember, could you tell us which other doctors were working at that time in your department and how many staff you had, how big the department was.

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: The department and ward actually had 50 beds. I don't know the exact number of nurses but there were certainly 15, headed by a head nurse which had a higher training level, and there was Dr. Simic, Dr. Slavica Jevtovic who will be coming after me, there was myself, and there was another -- a man called Zoran Dimitrijevic, I think he was still there. I don't think there were any other doctors. Yes, there were, there was Rada -- what was her surname? -- Rada Bukvic, and she is still there. Of course, there was social workers, there was a psychologist, but they were auxiliary educators or people who assisted us in our diagnosis and therapy, and of course, there was a working therapist as well; I forgot him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that Dr. Simic was a young doctor at the time and Dr. Slavica Jevtovic?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: She was the mentor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Martinovic, in view of the fact that you were department head, did you personally have your own patients or was -- were the patients assigned to the other doctors in the department?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: I also had my own patients because it is a relatively small service, so I had time to have my own patients and I didn't want to give them up. I didn't want to give up having my own patients because it was important to me for my work that I continue as a working psychiatrist. But let me say that, as department head, I had to know each and every patient and they would always, during their doctor's rounds and other contacts and the mentor in charge of the doctor doing his specialist training, would always refer to me. So as head of department, I would have to know every single patient in my department and on the ward.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said, Doctor, as far as I understood, that sometime in 1991, your department was established when it was separated from neurology and became an independent, autonomous department; is that right? A separate department?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of the year we are interested in, 1992, as it was a year of various conflicts, was this reflected, were the general circumstances reflected on your department and especially so perhaps on your department or less than other departments?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: In psychiatry, we know that, in the course of direct stress, psychiatric disorders did not occur straight away. They usually occur once the stress has gone. So during the war in Bosnia, we didn't have many more patients coming in from the war zone, from that area. However, there were individual patients, such as Mitar, who, for various reasons, developed a psychotic disorder and, like anybody else, any other patients, he automatically ended up in the psychiatric department after being treated in the orthopaedic ward. But there weren't large numbers of people coming in at that time yet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understand your answer to my question, you said that there was a delayed action and that psychological disorders and the stress that caused them were manifest later on; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Martinovic, you mentioned a moment ago, and I would like to -- you mentioned him a moment ago but let me ask you, do you remember patient Mitar Vasiljevic from 1992? And if you do, tell us what you can remember about him before we show you some documents which I will ask explanations about. But first of all, tell us what you remember with respect to the patient.

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the patient at all. I absolutely do not remember him. We have many people coming in, and from the medical documents, I can just read what it says there but I have no direct recollection of him, no, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he was not one of the patients that you said were your personal patient?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: No, he was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please wait for me to complete my question before you give an answer. So he was not one of your personal patients, the patients that you were in charge of personally?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: No, he was not my patient.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you now have a look at the case history of Mitar Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown Exhibit 138.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Martinovic, would you take a look at the first page, please, with the general data.

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a doctor who worked there at the time and as the head of department who probably came into contact with case histories of this type, could you tell me what you see from this case history with respect to patient Mitar Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I can see -- I don't want to repeat the dates, you all know them, but that he was treated in -- at two departments, the orthopaedic department and the psychiatric department. The final diagnosis was 298.9, and the signature were the doctors on duty, Dr. Simic from psychiatry and Dr. Jovicevic from orthopaedics. Everything else is clear: What was done; the surgical interventions at the orthopaedics department and, of course, treatment at the psychiatric department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you have a look at what your doctors or your department noted down and the importance of it.

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: He was transferred to our department on the 8th of July, 1992. Here and on the following page, it says that he was transferred by the neuropsychiatrist on duty who was called in by the orthopaedist because his behaviour was conspicuous and that kind of behaviour required a psychiatric examination. On the following day, my colleague under whose patient he was - because the doctor who transferred him was neurology, from the neurological department, and we were all on duty, both neurology and psychiatry. So he appeared on the 8th of July, Dr. Simic was in charge of the patient, he came under Dr. Simic, and Dr. Simic describes here that he was in a very agitated, restless state. He describes the patient as singing, shouting, resisting personnel, it was difficult to establish contact, and so on and so forth, which meant that it was a very seriously disturbed patient due to a psychosis which existed. I don't know whether you have the temperature chart and the therapy medicines chart because if I were to look at the temperature chart and the therapy sheet, I would be able to see he probably got neuroleptic, strong neuroleptic therapy, which would be a sign that he was highly distressed, so if I would look at the temperature chart and therapy sheet, I would be able to tell you that more exactly. After receiving therapy, the patient calmed down and in the decursus, or repeated examination on the 15th of July, it states that he was calmer, his behaviour was adequate so that was the decursus morbi on the 15th of July. Then we take the wife's statement, the heteroanamnesis from the wife, as we call it, and she explains what he was like, what his behaviour was like before he came into hospital. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, I don't think we need all of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I don't think we have a temperature chart but we certainly have the medicines that he was on in some other exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, it will be the next exhibit, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Martinovic, if I have understood you correctly, he was examined by the neuropsychiatrist who was not working at your own department but was a psychiatrist from neurology; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and that's his signature, Bora Bogdanovic, I've known him for 30 years or more. Unfortunately, he is no longer amongst us. That is clear here, on the 7th of July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise the remark made by Dr. Bogdanovic?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely so, and I know his handwriting very well. I know him very well and I know his handwriting very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So on the 7th of July, Dr. Bogdanovic wrote down those remarks. Would you read out what it says for the 8th of July. I don't think you interpreted the date of Mitar Vasiljevic's transfer to your department correctly.

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: It says here that on the 7th of July, he was examined by the neuropsychiatrist on duty and that he wrote "Transfer the patient to the psychiatric department." The next piece of information that I can see from this is that, on the 8th of July, the first comment was made as to the objective psychiatric finding, which was when the psychiatrist came on duty the following day, he probably got the patient to examine. So that's one day. So if he was transferred, probably it was in the afternoon because the doctor on duty works in the afternoon and during the night. So if on the 7th of July, he was transferred to the psychiatric department and that the doctor on duty gave him drugs, when Dr. Simic came to work the next day, he took the patient over and wrote down the 8th of July. I think that's clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember whether the 7th of July was a national holiday?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the 7th of July, at the time, was a national state holiday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should now like to ask you to take a look at the therapy chart.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And would the doctor be shown document P165, please.

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: May I comment? May I make a comment?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please, but slowly for the interpreters and because of any medical terms that you might come across. So nice and slowly, please, along with your comments. What does the therapy sheet tell you?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: We can see here that a neuroleptic therapy was ordered, prescribed, which is administered to the most disturbed patients. It is Topral. Topral is a very strong neuroleptic, and the dose was very high, four times one tablet a day up until the 12th. What is that, July? Are we talking about July? Nozinan, another neuroleptic, on the 9th the dosage was increased to three times 100 milligrams. And let me say that Topral is administered intramuscularly, which means it is a serious therapy, and Nozinan was in the form or tablets. Quite obviously, looking at this therapy sheet, we can see that he was exceptionally disturbed, probably fixed - tied up - we sometimes have to fix the patient to prevent injury. They are not usually dangerous, but to prevent them from injuring themselves. So quite certainly, it was a very serious psychotic disorder which, luckily, quieted down after four or five days. The only thing that could have been given was intravenous application of drugs but that is risky business and we tend to avoid it. That was the only other thing that could have been done, but what was administered and prescribed was sufficient and, as we can see, the patient responded to the therapy and did calm down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you had a look at the therapy list to the end, towards the end of treatment, what was prescribed, according to the therapy chart? Were there any deteriorations or were drugs increased at a certain point, anything like that?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we can see that on the 19th, there was a relapse, probably, because the Largactil therapy was increased to 200 milligrams, which is an exceptionally high dosage, and that went on for -- that went on until the 27th when it was reduced again to three times 100 milligrams. So there was a relapse episode where the condition deteriorated and, according to this, it lasted 6, 7, no, as much as 10 days, I see from the therapy chart. With psychosis, that is quite possible and does occur in the course of treatment despite the therapy. The process is repeated; the patient becomes very disturbed and we have to increase the doses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Martinovic, according to what you have seen in the therapy chart, you consider that the dosages were very high to begin with, which indicates the seriousness of the disorder that the patient was suffering from, Mitar Vasiljevic. Have I understood your answer properly?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. It is a sure sign of a very serious psychotic condition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to the drugs administered, the doses were increased again, and from that, you deduced that his condition must have deteriorated. Dr. Martinovic, would you now please have a look at the discharge sheet from your department. It is Exhibit D30 or D30.1.

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Have you got a question for me?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Would you look at this document, which I think has your signature as department head. Could you comment on that document?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: It gives the time spent in hospital and the diagnosis; psychosis 298.9. At that time, according to psychiatric nomenclature, is a code which denotes a psychotic disorder without precisely defining the entity of the disorder. I have to say in the doctrine of psychiatry, diagnosis are never written -- let me explain it this way: If a patient comes in to us for the first time with a schizophrenic picture, we are sure that it is the initial schizophrenic onset but we never write down that diagnosis because the man might never suffer from this psychosis again but we don't want to burden the patient with a diagnosis which will stay with him for the rest of his life, so that is psychiatric doctrine. We never do that to begin with. So in this case, looking at this case, we were not able to reach the right diagnosis, that is to say, to differentiate the exact group, so we put a general psychotic group. We classed into a general psychotic group and gave it that general psychotic code. For you to be able to understand this better, the most important symptom of a psychosis is the patient's lack of contact or loss of contact with reality and that is what Mitar Vasiljevic suffered from. Let me also say that diagnosis in psychiatry is also a function of time so a diagnosis is not static, it is dynamic. A psychiatric diagnosis is dynamic and if symptoms are manifest, then the diagnosis becomes crystalised, so you never put the ultimate diagnosis first, you wait to see the patient's development and manifestation of the disorder before a final ultimate diagnosis is written down. We have the description of his behaviour here when he was brought in; after prescribed therapy, it says that his condition improved; and it is important to note that he was discharged at the request of his spouse, which means that the physician did not consider that the time was -- had come for him to go home. The doctor would usually have kept a person suffering from this kind of condition at the psychiatric ward for a month or two, but the wife, for some reason, asked that he be released, and so with her signature and on her responsibility, he was released. This shows that three times 100 milligrams of a drug was to be -- of Largactil, was to be taken by the patient in future. This is a very large dosage, which shows that he should not have been discharged at that time. It is a large dose to be taken in an outpatient form. And of course, he was told to come back for a control examination in 14 days' time and was accorded sick leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Martinovic, you told us when you gave your curriculum vitae that you have been a forensic expert in Yugoslavia for many years. You have seen diagnosis and the other information that you had in front of you. Since you did not participate in the actual treatment of Mitar Vasiljevic, can you, on the basis of what you just saw, describe his mental state of health, as a forensic expert, at the time he was first examined by a psychiatrist? Was he a responsible person or not, and to what degree, of course, if you're able to do so?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: As I have been a forensic expert, I know very well what competence means. So as to avoid any confusion, competence is always evaluated for a particular crime. There is no general incompetence, but Mitar's condition was such that qualifies him as a man who was outside reality, which means that he had an actual interruption in his contact with reality from the moment he entered the hospital. This probably started much earlier, in orthopaedics, but they didn't recognise it. So he was outside reality. If he were to commit a crime, then he probably would not have been considered competent, but I must underline that competence is always evaluated in relation to a particular criminal offence. There is no such thing as general incompetence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Martinovic, could you please examine another exhibit that we have here, P162, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 162.1 is the B/C/S version to be shown to Witness Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look at it, it is a letter.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, 161.1. 161.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you been able to read through the letter? After all, it's in handwriting. You see from the contents that it was written by Mitar Vasiljevic on the 13th of July, 1992, that is at the time that he was in your department, and it appears to have been addressed to Dr. Slavica Jevtovic. In view of the contents of the letter, could you tell us something, first in general terms, about this letter. How do you view it as a psychiatrist?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, on the 13th of July, he was already sedated. This can be seen from the temperature chart, and the fact that he wrote a letter, it happens quite frequently among patients to address doctors in this way, with a letter. The letter is quite realistic. He says how he took some candy without paying for it, then he's saying that he asked for it on trust and, of course, he pledges that it was not stolen, that he just borrowed it, but after all, there's something that deviates from normal behaviour. Someone can't take some candy from a shop and tell the salesperson, whom he doesn't know, that he's taking it on credit and that he will pay for it later. In the second part of the letter, again, it reflects inadequate behaviour because if he has some physical illnesses, he could normally tell the doctor and ask for an examination. However, here, he says that he will go on a hunger strike, which is quite inadequate in relation to his request. And the last sentence is pathognomonic; it is indicative of a disturbance, and he says, "I would like to ask you also to tie my arms and legs." This is an interesting phenomenon that we encounter in the case of highly agitated patients who, themselves, in spite of the drugs they are taking, ask to be tied down, and this restlessness that they feel is most unpleasant for them and, if they are tied down, then there is a possibility that they will calm down as a result of that too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, on the first page, when he says that he wanted to take the candy on his honesty, as he puts it, that on trust, but that -- that he was checking out the salesman, as if he had the money but he wanted to check out the salesman and his honesty; is that a normal reaction, especially by a person who had a similar profession?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: To check out the salesman, well, that, too, is an indication of inadequate behaviour. Why should he check out the salesman? This is nothing to do with the honesty of the salesman or his ability to check him out, so this is also an indication of disturbed behaviour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Martinovic, you have seen some of these documents. You have seen how Mitar Vasiljevic was transferred to your department. In view of the fact that this was a wartime year and that you had many reservists; is it possible for this patient to be one who was faking illness so as to avoid going to war and having to fight? Because such a suspicion has been expressed. Would that be possible, on the basis of what you now know about his disease?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Psychiatry as a medical science is a very precise science. Believe me, in my career of almost 40 years, I haven't come across a single malingerer. You know, we often say, talking loosely, he's pretending, he's faking, but only a person of low intelligence can fake Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. something because he cannot judge whether he will succeed or not so somebody who is only insane can try. In this particular case, in the case of Mitar, it is absolutely impossible for him to have tried to simulate a mental disease first because of -- I've already given the first reason -- and secondly because we would all immediately recognise it. There was not just Dr. Simic, who was a beginner, but there was his mentor, there was me. I must have been involved in the therapy, in the prognosis and diagnosis, also regarding the time of discharge. So I can say with emphasis that it is absolutely impossible that Mitar could have faked his disease.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Martinovic. Let me ask you something else. We have some data and written evidence that Mitar Vasiljevic underwent treatment for alcoholism and he has been suspected of being an alcoholic. To what extent could that effect, if at all, his mental disorder? Are the two directly related, not related, or it may have a certain degree of influence?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Alcoholism is a condition resulting from excessive use of alcohol over a long period of time and it can be a good basis for psychiatric disorders. In this particular case, there is no clear indication that alcoholism was the exclusive reason of the psychotic disease but it could have, to some extent, contributed to the psychosis. If he had not been an alcoholic, the psychosis may not have set in. Alcoholic psychoses are quite clear, they can clearly be diagnosed. Alcoholism is easily recognizable among people, but in answer to your question, alcohol was not the only reason of this psychotic condition but it could have contributed to its development but we can't know that nor to what extent it could have contributed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Martinovic, mental disorders of this kind, can they be inherited? Can they be traced back to ancestors, to parents? If you had some indication of that, would that be relevant, the fact that Mitar's mother was a mental patient, that she had tried to commit suicide and actually committed suicide and died when Mitar was young? If we had any such information, could that have an impact? I apologise, you have to wait now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Where is there any evidence of that, Mr. Domazet? I don't recall your client mentioning a word of it. Is that the basis of your objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it appears that Mr. Domazet is testifying at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll tell you, Your Honour, and it is up to you to judge whether it is quite true. Not only has Mitar Vasiljevic failed to say that in answer to my questions and the questions of the Prosecution, but he did say that his mother died when he was a little boy, but this is information that I obtained from the psychiatrist, Dr. Lopicic, who talked to him in the detention unit and to whom he told these details and he said that he concealed it because it was considered shameful for the whole family that anything like that happened. So he never told me that, in spite of the many conversations that we have had, and that is how I learnt about this. I really, at this point in time, have no other source, though probably I could reach a proper source because he obviously concealed this for reasons of his own, but it is well-known that these kind of things, like mental disease and suicide, are considered tragedies and a disgrace for the family so I assume that was the only reason. But he did tell us that his mother died when he was a little boy and I have just told you how I learnt about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Domazet, that's very interesting, but nevertheless you are not giving evidence. You are going to call Dr. Lopicic, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. May I put this question as a hypothetical one? If there was such an incident in Mitar Vasiljevic's family, could that have any bearing as something, an inheritance factor, a hereditary factor?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, we still haven't seen her report, of course. I hope we're going to see it soon. Assuming that she is going to give that as a hearsay piece of evidence, there is a problem then, of course, as to the weight to be given to it but it would enable you, if you undertake to call her to say that, that she was told by your client this, then you are permitted to ask the doctor this question. But all of your explanations and your thoughts about the circumstances are not evidence, I want to make that very, very clear, and all of that explanation that you have given to us, we must ignore in relation to the weight to be given to Dr. Lopicic's evidence of a hearsay statement by your client. I'll see whether, in the circumstances, Mr. Groome still maintains his objection. With that undertaking, Mr. Groome, I think that it's admissible; what weight we give to it is another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think that Dr. Martinovic, as one of the doctors responsible for his care, it's certainly proper to ask him if Mr. Vasiljevic said anything of this nature to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But simply as a legal question, if he undertakes to call a doctor to give hearsay evidence as to what she was told by the accused, that would make this question admissible, but I emphasise, the weight we give to it is a different matter. But can you suggest that he should not be entitled to ask the question on that undertaking?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The only thing I would add, Your Honour, it was my understanding that Dr. Martinovic was not being called as an expert to answer such hypothetical questions but rather as the person who actually provided care for Mr. Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: He says that he can't remember him and I doubt whether he will be able to give us any evidence of anything other than that which is written down. But he is an expert. I don't know, I haven't seen his statement or whether this was in his statement or not, or whether you've been given fair warning of it, but I'm still anxious to know if you've got any legal basis for an objection still if we have the undertaking that that hearsay evidence will be produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not have any previous statement of Dr. Martinovic. The only thing I do have is a one-sentence summary in the 65 ter submissions, saying that he would testify about Mr. Vasiljevic's mental condition at the time that he was treated, so this is a surprise to me that he's going to be asked such hypothetical questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, you are building up a case in reply as it goes, I'm afraid, but you will be able to obtain from your doctor this -- his or her reaction to this evidence. Well, Mr. Domazet, it produces a number of practical problems but, legally, it must be admissible. It is a shame, if I may say so, that we were not given -- or the Prosecution was not given fair warning of this. When are we going to get her report?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I can say, Your Honour, is that I spoke to her last night. She's working on the report. I can tell you, if that is of any interest to you, what the conclusions will be. Of course, she will provide the explanations. Judging by what she told me, the conclusion will be that Mitar Vasiljevic, at the time he was hospitalised, was an incompetent person and who could not control his behaviour but that, in the period relevant for the indictment, the June, that he had diminished competence. To what degree, that will probably be explained in her report, so according to her finding, which I hope we will receive by the end of the week, it is diminished responsibility in the relevant period covered by the indictment. I don't know whether I have answered your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I am probably only repeating myself but, Mr. Domazet, this is an appalling way of running the case. There has been no notice given under the Rules. You were required to give it a long time ago. This is an issue which arose a very long time ago. It is making it very difficult for the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber to deal with these sorts of things but that is what we will deal with when we get the report, and I am grateful that you have told us what we are likely to see in it, but it is not, if I may say so, a good picture so far as efficiency is concerned. You ask the question of the doctor and we'll proceed from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Martinovic, my question was a disorder of this kind, could there be a hereditary factor involved if any such disorder or disease existed in one of the parents?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely so. Psychiatry today attaches increasing importance to hereditary factors and it is well-known in our practice that psychosis can be traced through several generations. If it is true that his mother committed suicide and that she had, prior to that, made several attempts to do so, then it is highly probably that she was a mentally-disturbed person, and under those conditions in Bosnia, she was probably never examined or treated and this ended, tragically, with her suicide. And if this fact were true and if I were to know it as a psychiatrist, it would be very important for me in establishing the diagnosis and for the prognosis. If there is such a powerful hereditary factor, the very fact of suicide itself need not mean so much, but if there were several attempts and a suicide at the end, this is certainly a symptom of a mental disorder. What kind, I can't say, of course, now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Dr. Martinovic. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome. Cross-examined by Mr. Groome:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Martinovic, my name is Dermot Groome and I will be asking you some questions for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, let me ask you about this hereditary matter that has just come up. From what you say, it seems that it is -- could be of important or significant diagnostic -- or would have significance for diagnostic purposes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, given the significance that it would have, shouldn't we expect to see somewhere in the medical records or in the interview of Mrs. Vasiljevic some questions or some attempt by Dr. Simic or the other doctors to explore this, to explore the mental history of the family?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely so. It is a question which a psychiatrist always asks his patient, whether there have been any mental disorders in the family, whether there was suicides. Those are practically compulsory questions. Now, why that is not included in this case history, if I may, I can make an assumption. What Defence counsel said, in our country, it is something that is very often hidden, even in such serious situations where husbands are undergoing treatment. This is just in the realm of speculation and a hypothesis that she didn't give the proper answer. Of course, Dr. Simic didn't say: "I asked her if there were any cases of suicide in the family or psychosis in the family," and she said, "No." We don't write that, we just say what the patient did say, so the positive response. But as I say, that is a compulsory question and I don't think he didn't ask it. I cannot believe that he didn't ask it. Whether she answered is another matter, and what she said is another matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me see if I'm understanding you correctly. It seems what you're saying is that you're quite confident that the doctors did ask questions regarding family mental history but that the fact that there's nothing recorded in the record, it appears that they were told, the doctors were told that there was nothing of significance in the family mental history; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely so. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it appears the first indication that we have of some previous mental history which could have impact on a finding of Mr. Vasiljevic's competence was brought to light this past weekend in an interview with a psychiatrist by the name of Dr. Lopicic; correct? I need to have you answer yes or no, for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. A talk with a psychiatrist tete-a-tete, like the Scheveningen one, opens up -- as we say, people open up their souls. If she has established a good emotional link with the patient, then he could have told her much more than his Defence counsel or even here in the courtroom. It is an intimate atmosphere, where the patient opens up, opens his heart and soul, and possibly he said that for the first time then and had not mentioned that before and hence the Defence counsel never heard about it. That is possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, this opening of the soul that you talk about, would you agree with me that, that in the course of therapy, a patient learns to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. trust their psychiatrist and, over the course of time, reveals more and more information about what's troubling them and their previous history; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. This was not possible in the first stage while he was agitated and the large quantity of drugs that he was prescribed, but 10 or 15 days later, yes, he could have given much more information if he had been asked and we could have learned much more. That is what we usually do to substantiate our objective findings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And wouldn't it be reasonable for us to assume that Mr. Vasiljevic was more inclined to trust and be open with the psychiatrists over his three-week course of treatment in Uzice than in a single meeting with a psychiatrist for the first time last week?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: I think it is possible because the lady doctor probably talked to him at length. She used all her methods, it is a short period of time, but she was able to establish a transfer relationship, that is to say, the emotional relationship between patient and physician. And I think it is absolutely possible. She managed to get that feedback whereas the doctor in Uzice didn't. Perhaps he didn't ask him the way she did. He should have -- not should have, he absolutely certainly should have. But the doctor in Uzice had before him a very highly-agitated patient. He was not able to talk to him for seven or eight days. His condition had calmed down and what was important for the doctor, that the patient was calm and that the psychosis had calmed down. So maybe he didn't go into a further exploration. The important thing was that the worst was over. He was able to contend the worst, the dramatically psychotic stage, which was quite certainly present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: And after that, it calmed down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this letter that was written, P161, that was written to a Dr. Slavica -- and I forget her last name, but the letter is just to your left there. Would you agree with me that, from the tone of that letter, we could conclude that he had some type of trusting relationship with this female psychiatrist?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. That is why he addresses her, because she was Dr. Simic's mentor. He was a doctor specialising in psychiatry and she was the mentor and present during the examinations and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I think you were very candid with us at the start of your testimony, saying that you have no direct recollection of Mitar Vasiljevic whatsoever. Everything you've told us has been based upon your review of the records; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've told us how important it is to keep detailed records and that is something you've tried to instill in the people that work under you; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely correct, because I'm also a forensic expert.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were asked to give a conclusion regarding your experience or expertise in forensic psychology and you said that you did not believe Mr. Vasiljevic was competent, legally competent during the time he was in your ward. What I want to ask you is would you consider everybody that has a diagnosis of 298.9, would everybody who has that diagnosis be considered legally incompetent, in your expertise?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise to this august Tribunal but I have to say -- tell you the basics in forensic expertise, in psychiatry. Competence is determined for a concrete crime, criminis in tempore -- I think I've got it right. At the time a crime was committed, for that particular act and crime, accountability and responsibility and competence are determined. So there isn't general incompetence or unaccountability. May I give you one example? If somebody has a -- suffers from schizophrenia and commits a crime within that disorder, he has the idea that his boss is abusing him and he kills his boss, that is completely incompetent. But if that same schizophrenic patient goes and robs a bank and takes money, then he is competent. He is responsible. The same patient doing two different things. So when you ask me whether he was competent when he was in hospital, if we're speaking about this, we must say what he did. During the time of treatment he did nothing. He's not in this court of law for that, for his time there. So I can only say hypothetically, in the condition he was in, agitated, for example, if he hit somebody and killed him while under this agitated condition, then that would be incompetent, unaccountable so that is how we assess competence and accountability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I suggest that you just put to the doctor the facts as you allege them to be that happened on the 14th of the month. I think it was what, 10 days before he went into the psychiatric ward.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. At this time, I'm just trying to explore what he based that conclusion on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, but You see, the doctor did mention that before and I've made a note, I was rather curious that he was able to say that he was incompetent to do anything without knowing what it was he was charged with, but that's a different matter. He did make the point that it had to be determined by reference to the particular acts which are alleged against him. I would be anxious to hear what he wants to say about what is alleged to have happened here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I don't know whether this takes it back as far as the shooting incident but that's another matter I suppose you will have to explore.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, given what you have seen before you in the medical records, are you able to give us any assessment or any opinion about an event that may have happened on the 14th of June?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: What happened then? I have no information about what happened on the 14th of June. It was one month before the disorder -- before the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is: --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, one month before the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you, through your assessment of the medical records that are before you, is it possible for you to give us any kind of opinion about an event that would have happened one month earlier, on the 14th of June?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: The information given by the wife in the case history indicates that it was a man with some sort of disturbed behaviour. If I remember correctly, it says he was nervous, he stayed at work longer than was necessary, that he couldn't keep to one place. He was restless, he kept going somewhere. He was hyperactive, as we psychiatrists would say; he couldn't sit still. But to reconstruct his psychological condition and state during that event, and I assume it was a crime that took place, is a very hypothetical business and I don't think I could and I don't think any expert would be able to assume what was going on at that particular moment, only if there were witnesses who could say what his conduct was like, then we could do a bit of reconstruction but otherwise, it is difficult to say because it was one month before. But let me tell you something in general terms, psychoses never set out - how shall I put this? - like a flash of lightning, they never come suddenly, they always have a prehistory somewhere, going back a month, two months; something was happening. It needn't be remarked by his family members or even doctors. And his stay in the orthopaedic ward, where his behaviour was conspicuous, the doctors didn't realise straight away that it might be a psychological disturbance; they only called in the doctor, the psychiatrist, when the agitation had reached a peak. So it is difficult for me to assume, it would just be in the realm of hypothesis and I don't know if that would be useful to you, but in principle, in general terms, always -- or not always but mostly one would see signs a month or two prior to the actual psychosis becoming manifest, which is when the patient would go to hospital, so there might have been some signs along the way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you say that there may have been signs, that's very different than saying that somebody is disturbed enough that they might be incompetent; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It would be more along the lines of maybe somebody showing the initial signs of some physical disease but really not having the full-fledged disease until a month or two later; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. So his competence at the beginning and later on when he becomes psychotic, there's a big difference, so you have to look at it at the time the crime took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what I want to ask you is the diagnosis of 298.9, from what I understand you've told us, that is kind of a large group of unclassified types of psychoses; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely so, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just because somebody has -- has been diagnosed as that, doesn't mean that they are legally incompetent; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely correct. Incompetence is linked to the actual crime, directly linked to the actual crime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've looked over the therapy sheet and you've looked at the medicines that Mr. Vasiljevic was receiving. Those types of medicines in and of themselves don't indicate that he was incompetent, do they?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you a couple of questions about that letter. And you've read it now. The whole narration about the taking of the candy and whether it was right or wrong and whether to take it on trust, would you agree with me that that letter written on the 13th of July still shows that Mr. Vasiljevic, despite whatever mental disorder he was suffering, still had the capacity to distinguish between what is right and what is wrong? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: You know, if you're asking me about his ethical behaviour, then we psychiatrists never make a judgement as to ethics, whether people know what is right and wrong. But, if you're asking me cognitively whether he knew, he knew that something mustn't be taken without paying for it, he certainly knew that, although he was not in an actual psychotic state, and he says so, but his way of communicating with the salesperson and his behaviour indicate that there are disturbances. Everybody knows that you can't steal, you can't take something from somebody. So he says I'm going to take it and I haven't got the money now, so if you will trust me, I will pay for it later on. He wants to him to believe in his honesty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But cognitively, he knew that taking candy without paying for it would have been wrong; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely correct. He knows that he can't do that. And that's why he goes into his story of justification, I'll bring you the money, trust me, show confidence in me. But that is quite obviously inadequate behaviour. Regardless of the fact that he knows.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the other side of the letter, where there is this discussion about different physical ailments that he's feeling, and he makes a request to -- for treatment, would you agree with me that that shows that on the 13th of July, he was still capable of intentional, deliberate action? He was able to intend something and then to act in accordance with that intent?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. But his intention was not generally justified because if he says, if that is not done for him, he will go on a hunger strike. Can you imagine somebody who has come to a hospital for treatment says to the doctor, well, if you don't want to treat me, I'm going to go on a hunger strike. That is absolutely inadequate behaviour and indicates a disturbance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I believe when you described that letter, you used the word it was quite realistic, that it showed that he still, at the time he wrote this letter, was aware of reality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you know, in the condition he was in at the time he wrote the letter, he was coming back to reality. But I'm certain that in the first six or seven days when he was under that great therapy, he was absolutely outside reality. Now do you want me to explain what it means to be outside reality? But as his condition improved, and as he went to get the candies in the first place, quite obviously he was returning to reality, but not sufficiently. His explanations of his motives are unrealistic. He first says he wants the salesperson to trust him and that he would bring in the money. She probably said, "Well you have to pay," and was angry. In the second part of the letter, he threatens that he will go on a hunger strike for something very banal, which was an examination. So partially he is in reality and partially he is outside reality. If we can Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. say that; it's not the best illustration. But I -- what I want to say is that he still showed signs of behavioural disturbance, and this can be seen from the contents of the letter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, would you agree with me that, in the records that you have before you and that you've seen, that none of the doctors make a conclusion that he is outside of reality? They describe his agitation, his singing, his speech patterns, but there is no conclusion in any of the records saying he was outside of reality; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes. We don't write it down in the case history. I said "outside reality" to help the Court understand what a psychotic state and condition is. That is my explanation and it is an explanation given by psychiatry as the main explanation of psychosis is loss of contact with reality. You will find that in every psychiatric textbook, so that is something that a doctor does not mention right in the case history because it's not a component part of an objective psychiatric finding, it is only, if I can say that, a general rule of thumb for psychosis, this loss of sense of reality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, I want to ask you, aren't there specific psychoses that are related to hospitalisation? For example, a person who is not used to being confined to a particular area, can't psychoses set in when that person is confined to a very limited space and time for a long period of time?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. And it's a well-known phenomenon of penal psychosis, people who are in prison can be psychotic. But if you are asking about Mitar, he was not in a prison. A ward and department is a closed department, but it is not a prison. There are other people, other patients, other -- there is communication, there is trust. He knows it's a hospital. Perhaps he didn't know for the first five or six days, but, generally, he knew. And if you're asking me about Mitar, whether he could have entered a psychosis because he was in hospital, that is absolutely not possible. We have not had any cases recorded where somebody came to hospital and became psychotic. You know a hospital and a prison are not the same thing, I'm sure you will agree. In prison, we have what is called penal psychosis, that is a generally-known fact, but in this case, it could not have been that because it is not a prison. Psychosis can emerge in hospital as happened in the orthopaedic department. He was in the orthopaedic ward and a psychosis developed but not because he was in a closed space. And in orthopaedics, people come and go. He could go out -- he had a fractured leg, but he could go out any time. In our department, he can't go out; in the psychiatric department, he could only go out in the courtyard, for example.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Doctor, would it change your opinion if I were to tell you that he was in traction and could not leave his bed for a period of weeks, would that change your opinion as to whether his confinement to his bed could have been a contributing factor to the psychosis which was observed in your department? And let me couple that with we've heard testimony here that he was being regularly teased by other patients and possibly even some members of staff regarding how he received his injury. Could they have been contributing factors to his condition?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: I must go back to your first question. I understood you to say that you thought that psychosis can break out because it was a confined space and a movement was restricted, what I compared to penal psychosis. But when you asked me whether that could activate a psychosis, that is absolutely possible and let me explain why. I assume on the basis of scant information that his wife gave us that he was in a state of increased activity and this can be seen most often with what we call manic psychosis, manic depressive or just manic, a manic episode. And when you tie a patient like that, and he was fixed because of his traction, he had to be still, kept still, and psychologically and psychiatrically he was disturbed, he was in what we call the plus phase of hyperactivity, hyperspeech, everything was hyper, insomnia sets in and so on, possibly the fact that he was tied up could have contributed to the outbreak of this psychosis. That is absolutely possible and it is highly probable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that when somebody is transferred into the psychiatric ward, that they are given a psychiatric exam; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what would be the standard battery of psychological tests that are administered to a patient being admitted to your ward in 1992?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: It's like this; standard tests don't exist in an objective psychiatric examination. If the need for tests arises, we send them to a psychologist, who performs those tests. For us to reach a diagnosis, the initial diagnosis, the first diagnosis, and the need for hospitalisation and treatment in the psychiatric department is a psychiatric examination is enough, and there are no tests there. They are in the following, first of all: The physician gets information from the people, the staff of the orthopaedics department, and they tell him he shouted, he swore, he does -- has refused to take his medicines. He is making the general chaos on the department, that is the first piece of information. Next, the psychiatrist sees the patient. He sees that he is agitated, he is not responding properly to questions or whatever. There are a few questions that we do ask. I don't want to tire you with that. For example, we ask him, "Do you hear voices? Does somebody wish to poison you?" a few questions of that kind, and on the basis of that, we reach a diagnosis, the doctor doing the examination reaches a diagnosis and decides whether to move the patient to the psychiatric ward. I always thought that, with any disorder, for example, a fracture, if he is tied and showing psychotic signs, I usually say, "Send him over to us," and then we give him therapy. I always insist it. If a patient was showing psychotic symptoms, transfer him to psychiatry. There was less chance of him injuring himself. There were people who jumped out of the window, I know cases of that kind, people who jumped out of a window, and that's very dramatic when you get that type of case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Doctor, this initial diagnosis based on this test, where would that be recorded? Would that be recorded on the case history somewhere?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: You mean the doctor that said he should be transferred to psychiatry, that doctor, before psychiatry?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, whatever doctor would have administered this test and asked these questions. Would that doctor not have recorded the results of that examination somewhere on the medical record?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, that is not customary. He just wrote down, as far as I remember, "Transfer the patient to the psychiatric ward." There's no diagnosis by that doctor. And he signed it. I know the way he works. I've worked with that doctor for 30 years. I personally, when I go, I do write a diagnosis but some physicians don't write their diagnosis, they say, "Transfer the patient to the psychiatric department," and then leaves it to us, and as I can see, there isn't a diagnosis there, and that's how that particular doctor used to work. He would refer him to the psychiatric department, and he wasn't duty-bound to write down the diagnosis. He works in neurology whereas we psychiatrists are better able to write down and reach a diagnosis. And the diagnosis isn't important. The important thing is he is psychotic, showing psychotic symptoms and has to be referred to psychiatry. Perhaps the doctor on duty that day had a lot of other business to attend to. So he would have to -- the patient was transferred to psychiatry for the therapy to be prescribed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We'll adjourn until 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, I want to just pick up where we left off and we were talking about an initial diagnosis. My question to you is, wouldn't it be necessary to at least have a provisional diagnosis of a patient before one could decide what medications and other therapies would be appropriate for that patient?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: The practice in psychiatric treatment is, of course, to bear in mind the diagnosis, but what is most important is the so-called syndrome approach, which means if a patient is restless, regardless of which disease he has, a certain medication is administered. If it's schizophrenia, manic depressive, or this general psychosis. Therefore, the drug depends on the symptoms and the diagnosis is not so important. It is important to remove the symptoms. If somebody has hallucinations, he gets the appropriate drugs. If someone is agitated, again, he gets the appropriate medicines. Of course, the diagnosis is important for the verification of the disease, and for future prognosis. I think I've made myself clear. It's the symptom that matters at first, not the diagnosis, as a sign of the disease.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it common that -- well, we know that the discharge diagnosis in this case was 298.9, and we know that that is a group of unclassified psychoses. My question to you is: Is it common for a patient to be discharged from the ward under this classification which is essentially a nonclassification? Is that common?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, and it happens very frequently. At the beginning of my testimony, I said that in psychiatry, a diagnosis is established along the way, so in hospital, it may be diagnosed as 298.9, and then a month later, it might be 295.0, schizophrenia or depressive psychosis, so the diagnosis is not established as in somatic, physical disease. Even then, it can't always be established at once but almost always over a certain period of time, following the so-called horizontal course of the disease, so it's quite possible that the diagnosis be established after several months and that is why we have this general basket into which all the psychoses are put when we don't know exactly which one it is. And the practice is that it's better not to establish schizophrenia at first contact with the patient but that that diagnosis be established during the second or third course of treatment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, after the initial examination of a patient by a doctor on your ward, is there a set protocol of continued examinations or continued evaluative steps?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: In this specific case, the intern admitted the patient, examined him, established some sort of a diagnosis of his own, and his own therapy. As he was still studying, he had to consult his mentor - in this case, Dr. Slavica Jevtovic - and together with her, to explore the condition of the patient to establish some kind of initial hypothetical diagnosis which is probable but not 100 per cent certain. In this case, the patient was tied up, a large quantity of medicines, so he was not suitable for further exploration for the first week or so because there's no verbal communication, or at least, very limited verbal communication, so I believe that for the first six or seven days, he didn't make any further explorative examinations, apart from what he was able to see; his restlessness and so on. So the first control check-up was done after five, six days and we see in the case history that he had quietened down which, of course, doesn't mean that there was no psychosis, and we can see that, judging by the therapy given. We even see that there was a relapse after that. The procedure is that this intern, together with his mentor, establish the final diagnosis, in this case, 298.9, that he should consult her over the medicines, whether he needs to be put on sick leave - because I assume he was involved in the wartime operations, I don't know what he was doing - and to see with the mentor and the head of department, most frequently with the head of department as well, though this is not obligatory but, in most cases, he is consulted, especially if it's something complicated. Sometimes the whole team in the department, including the social worker and the psychologist, if it's something complicated, has to be consulted. But as a matter of routine, the doctor and the mentor of that doctor are consulted, after which he is treated as an outpatient.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, that was actually my next question. Are there periodic consultations where the key medical staff meet to discuss a particular patient, and if so, how often are they held; once a week? How often are they held?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Consultations in complicated cases when things are not clear are scheduled for each individual patient if there is a need to do so. I think in practice, this would be once or twice a week for the 50 or so patients because most of them are quite clear cases. Frequently, they are recidivists, patients who have been treated for years and we recognise them as soon as they walk through the door so there are no consultations. So we have consultations once or twice a week for so-called borderline Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. cases between psychosis and neurosis and when the diagnosis is not clear. In this case, in Mitar's case, the diagnosis was so clear that consultations of a team were not required. His doctor and his mentor was sufficient and, of course, the head of the department and other doctors making the daily rounds in the morning would see him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, could you tell us what the symptoms of delirium tremens are?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. I think I have treated at least 1.000 such cases in these 30 years. It is a very frequent disease in our country, an area in which people drink a lot. They drink slivovitz, brandy, especially at the time when plum brandy is being made. Though more recently, in the last few years, there are fewer such cases. So I am very familiar with this and I can tell you if you are interested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please tell us what are the symptoms of delirium tremens.

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Delirium tremens is a brief mental disorder that develops exclusively in alcoholics. It consists of the following: First of all, the patient most frequently suffers from insomnia, fear, and hallucinations. Hallucinations are typical in this stage of visual optical hallucinations, so he most frequently sees small animals; ants, worms, flies that he tries to shake off. He asks for assistance to get rid of them. Then there is a lack of orientation, disorientation in time and space; he doesn't know where he is nor what the time is. And also in relations with other people, he is disoriented very frequently; he doesn't know that he is in hospital, he doesn't know why he's there, what's wrong with him, a total loss of touch with reality. And if you're also interested, they can be very suggestive. You give him a piece of paper and read what it says and he'll start reading from a blank page. So he's extremely restless, very frequently you have to give a certain medicine intravenously and, thank God, nowadays there's a drug called Heminervin which removes the psychosis in a day or two so that nowadays it's not a serious problem. And there's a very pronounced tremor. That's why it's called tremens, the whole body shakes and the hands and the sweating. So it's a very dangerous situation. In a certain percentage of cases, it ends in death, it can be fatal. So as I have said, in a day or two, it can be treated and it is most welcome for the benefit of the patient.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, it seems from your description of delirium tremens that, at least to some extent, the symptoms of delirium tremens overlap with the symptoms of the psychosis you've described Mr. Vasiljevic as having; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But the difference is enormous.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how would you characterise the difference?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Let me explain. In Vasiljevic's case, there was no tremens, no trembling of the body, no perspiration, no hallucinations, which are typical of delirium tremens, so that is quite sufficient for me to say it was not delirium, it's an acute psychosis. What is common to both is loss of orientation. Vasiljevic didn't know where he was nor what was happening nor who was around him. Verbal communication was also something that it was difficult to establish with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, would it change your opinion or your conclusion that you've just given us if you knew that prior to this hospitalisation, Mr. Vasiljevic had, on several other occasions, been treated by a neuropsychiatrist for delirium tremens and that, just prior to his hospitalisation, he was using a great deal of alcohol, would that change your conclusion of whether that, at least in some part, some of his symptoms could have been attributed to delirium tremens?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. It is so different that there is absolutely no possibility of me making a mistake and saying psychosis instead of delirium tremens. As I said a moment ago, for tremens, you give intravenous medicines. In Vasiljevic's case, very powerful neuroleptics were administered which are exclusively given for psychosis, never for delirium tremens. It would be a terrible mistake for the doctor to make, not just he, but three or four of us. That is quite impossible. Delirium tremens is such a typical disorder that one simply cannot go wrong. Everything else could be questionable but not delirium tremens.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Re-examination, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Re-examined by Mr. Domazet:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Martinovic, linked to this last question by Mr. Groome, when you totally rejected, it seems to me, that this could have been delirium tremens but that it was a typical case of psychosis as you described it, does that change in any way your answer with respect to the influence of alcohol for the development of psychosis? Could we clear that up a little, if you will?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Regarding this point, I said, if you remember at the beginning, that alcoholism could have been a sort of basis for the development of psychosis. It is highly probable that he - I've also said that - that he was in a plus stage, as we call it, for a month or two prior to hospitalisation and, of course, he drank excessively, then he came to orthopaedics because of his fracture, which can always be a triggering factor for psychosis, a bodily injury can activate delirium tremens and other acute diseases. So I abide by what I said that alcohol could have had some effect on the outbreak of the disease and the clinical picture but I say again, delirium tremens is out of the question. It is quite impossible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Martinovic, answering Mr. Groome's question about what the doctor should have and probably did do to inquire about these things such as mental diseases in the family or suicides, you gave your answer and the questions mostly had to do with whether that information would be provided by the patient himself or his wife. So there were two possibilities for the doctor to learn about this; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to the patient himself, to what extent was he capable, in view of his condition at the time, and his answers even later with that regard? Were they relevant?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: For the first six or seven days, he couldn't say anything. I've already described the situation. He was out of touch with reality. He doesn't know what he's saying or where he is. After that, he could have said it but I am 100 per cent sure that Dr. Simic must have asked him that because the first thing we teach them when they start specialising is to ask relatives, including the patient, whether there are mental diseases in the family or suicides in your family. So I'm 100 per cent sure that he did ask him. Why he didn't write down the answer is because neither he nor his wife told him that. You see, even he refused to say anything about that to you and you have spent so much time with him. I was saying that, in our part of the world, suicide is a terrible act. It is anathema, you know, the attitude of religion towards it, and of course, mental disorders which are, regrettably still, considered a disgrace and he -- his mother lived in Bosnia where she probably never had any chance to see a psychiatrist and that is how she ended her life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was asking you this about him in person. So you said he could have said later but he also could have concealed it. Would that have had any effect, perhaps not on further treatment but would he have been kept in hospital longer? Because obviously both he and his wife wanted to shorten his stay in this hospital as much as possible because they asked to be discharged against doctors' advice. It's difficult to explore that further so I'll move on. As regards the wife, the only possibility that we did not consider is whether she, herself, knew as this was a long time prior to when they got married so that I really don't know whether she could have said anything.
