So this is a fact that you have no note of, nor do you recollect of ever hearing about it?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understood you, your answers correctly, when you were describing his competence at the time when you can speak of, that is, at the time he was being treated, you said that depended on the act and gave an example that if, in the course of hospitalisation, he were to hurt somebody physically or kill him, that he would not be competent but if he broke open a safe, that he would be considered competent. But would he be fully competent or reduced, would his competence be reduced? But that is also questionable, and you still stand by that answer?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Dr. Martinovic, I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor, for coming along to give evidence and for the evidence that you have given. You are now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Madam, will you please make the solemn declaration in the document which the usher is showing you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Please sit down. Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Mr. Domazet:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Jevtovic, good morning.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam Jevtovic, I will be examining you on behalf of the Defence counsel and will you please, when you hear my question, wait a few moments before giving your answer as we speak the same language and this is necessary to facilitate the simultaneous interpretation of your questions and answers. Also, in front of you, you have the screen with the transcript in English so you will see when the court reporters complete their recording of the translation, so please bear that in mind during your conversation. Will you please give us your basic particulars; your name, place and date of birth and your place of residence.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Slavica Jevtovic. By occupation, I am a neuropsychiatrist. I am living and working in Uzice. I have been working for 35 years. I was born in Osijek, in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam Jevtovic, you are working in the general hospital in Uzice?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since when have you been working in the hospital in Uzice?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I have been working continuously in Uzice since June 1966 and that is also the date when I started living in Uzice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that your -- what your occupation is, you're a doctor, a neuropsychiatrist. In which department are you working and have you been working at that department throughout?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: With the exception of a few months that a young doctor has to work as an intern, touring various departments, I have been continuously in the neuropsychiatric ward, and ten years ago when the university department was separated into psychiatry and neurology, I have been assigned to the psychiatric ward.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, as 1992 is relevant for us, could you tell us where you were working at that time.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I was working continuously in psychiatry. It is called the psychiatric service ever since 1991 to this day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please tell me, in 1992, what post you held, who was your superior, and who were the other doctors working with you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: In 1992, I was a specialist, holding the post of specialist. Our head of department was Dr. Borisav Martinovic. I had fellow specialists Bukvic and we had young doctors who had still not officially started their specialisation but were doctors' assistants as we called them, secondary doctors. And they were Dr. Simic and a lady doctor, Mirjana Perunicic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Jevtovic, was that sufficient for the task in hand at the time regarding the organisation of your department?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Quite certainly it was not sufficient, but I said that we had divided up into two services and the existing staff, specialist staff had to be divided up too, into two services. And that is why we employed new, young doctors, who were to begin their official specialist training and education, which they later did receive and graduated from. But of course it wasn't enough, it wasn't sufficient for, if I can say so, the misfortunes that were to engulf us. We had a lot of sick people coming Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. into our hospital from the whole of Bosnia, practically speaking, and this went on for several years. So in addition to our regular work, and we have a hospital section with 50 beds, and inpatients and we have a specialist outpatients department throughout the working hours every day. And we also had compulsory presence, or rather, shifts lasting 24 hours in the ward on the department. Because of that, we were forced as -- us older doctors had two specialisations, neurology plus psychiatry. For a long period of time, in fact, until three years ago, we were duty-bound to ensure -- to provide the second and third shifts. From the psychiatric department we could go and work -- we would go and work in the neurology department, and vice versa, the neurologists would come to do shifts in the psychiatric department, which made our work even more difficult because it is always easier to treat a patient for whom you admitted and are supervising his treatment rather than taking over a patient from a doctor who has just gone off duty and who you are replacing in the shift.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Jevtovic, you explained about the young doctors, Dr. Simic and Dr. Mirjana Perunicic, cases in point, that they were called secondary doctors. Now, my question is in concrete terms, Dr. Simic, did he have his patients and his department? Did they have their patients and departments? Were they doctors on the ward in the department?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: The department was not divided and the young doctors, on a regular basis, received patients but they didn't work independently, or autonomously, they worked under our supervision. And their status was what we called "secondary." Each senior physician was given an assignment by the head of the service, the head of the department, was given a doctor to supervise, to help him in reaching diagnoses, to help him in therapy, to help him in final diagnoses and writing the discharge sheet. But once these young doctors began their official specialist training, which was determined by the ministry of health, then they are ascribed an official mentor and that mentor is duty-bound to help the young physician in gaining the knowledge and training he needed in the field of psychiatry. And the mentor would have to confirm everything with his own signature. When the doctor enters into the second stage of specialist training, which he does at the institute in Belgrade -- that's where our young specialist doctors usually go to sit for their specialist final exams, they go to the institute in Belgrade to sit for that examination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Jevtovic, who was Dr. Simic's mentor at that time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I was his mentor. Before his specialist training and in the course of his specialist training, I was his official mentor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You explained that in your previous answer, but I should nonetheless like to ask you to explain to us what it actually meant in Dr. Simic's work. What did he have to consult to you about or what did he have to report back to you about and how did your relationship as mentor and doctor-trainee function?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: In practical terms, it was his duty to inform me everything about the patient and then, from time to time, I would talk to his patient to -- I would get an insight into all the documents, and I would give my agreement for therapy. We would discuss the diagnosis and what we call the differential diagnosis, all with the aim of his education and training in mind. There were doctor's rounds every day and we would all be present except the head of department who would be present on certain days but on others, he would have other things to attend to. Where we had exceptionally complicated, unclear cases, we would present the case before the head of department and all the doctors would take part in discussing that particular case together before the head of department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Explain to us about the rounds, doctor's rounds. You said they were daily rounds. Would you explain when the rounds took place, who would attend, and whether you moved from bed to bed or patient to patient. So could you tell us, in practical terms, what a doctor's visit or round consisted of.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will be happy to. A doctor's round is official and compulsory for all doctors in the department except the head of department. The head nurse is present as is a psychologist and the working therapist, and quite literally, we move from bed to bed each morning. We do our rounds very early on for practical reasons. First of all, our patients must receive therapy in time intervals and therefore have usually an 8-hour cycle. Secondly, this might sound a little strange to you, but they could get breakfast first in the morning because breakfast is distributed from the central kitchens to the wards and not everybody can receive breakfast at the same time. Our patients were not physically ill for the most part, and relatively they were younger people and they were hungry so they couldn't always wait for a late breakfast and dinner is 6.00 -- or 5.30 or 6.00. Neuroleptic drugs, the drugs that are used for mental patients, increase appetite, that is the first point. Secondly, we take in patients from the whole region and they don't have visits very often which means that their nearest and dearest and friends cannot bring food in. These people from Uzice are privileged in that way because visitors can bring in food so food is distributed at regular hours. In order to improve the food which, in recent years, was of a very poor quality, people would bring in extra food. If you have any more questions about doctor's rounds, please ask me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you and the other doctors, with the exception of the department head who didn't have to attend the rounds every day, you were duty-bound to see the patient at least once a day by his bed or in his bed, together with the doctor whose patient he was and all the other people you mentioned. Have I understood your answer correctly?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. The rounds include agreements about therapy and consultative examinations as well. The need to have consultative examinations are recorded by the head nurse in a separate notebook, a notebook of agreement, and then she phones up and calls the necessary specialists who we wish to consult. The daily rounds consist of short chats to the patient along with observation. We observe the behaviour and conduct of the patient, his ability to communicate with us and you can assess a great deal during that time. More detailed interviews and conversations are held separately in the doctor's office because there are some very interesting things that required discretion and confidentiality and we never discuss these things in the presence of other patients. I don't know how laymen imagine psychiatric wards to be. Psychiatric patients are not dislocated somewhere over there and that we doctors are in a sort of protected, separate place. The department and ward in which we are discussing in the period of 1992, it was a long barracks, linear in design, the rooms followed on one from another and then had you a doctor's office and dormitory and a doctor's office and a dormitory so nothing could happen in the department or on the ward without it being heard. Doctors' offices are not locked during working hours. Our patients have the freedom to move around within the department and ward. It is locked to the outside, but patients can come into the doctor's office any time they like. Whether they stay a longer or shorter period of time will depend on the doctor's requirements, whether he is scheduled for an interview with the patient on that day. But very often the patient, especially at the beginning of the treatment, has a great need to see his therapist because the greatest problem and basic symptom are anxiety and fear. Sometimes they come and say, "Just let me sit there for a while, please, Doctor, sit with you." They don't have to talk to you. So they are not separate. They are not isolated, they are not closed off anywhere as far as we and the rest of the staff are concerned. Second, the modern approach to psychiatry is the principle of a treatment through a therapy community. All persons employed, the whole staff and the patients, form one large group and each patient, depending on his condition and state takes part in the work of the department as a whole.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: The president of the therapy community is elected each week. Certain days are designated where we all meet together to talk about the life of the patient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Madam, I'm sorry to interrupt but you are causing troubles for the interpreters you are speaking so quickly. So slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Jevtovic, you have heard the remarks, just a little slower, please. And may we focus on my questions and I shall be asking you additional questions for additional explanations, if the need arises, to prevent long answers to my questions and I'm sure we'll cover everything that is necessary. If I understood you correctly and what you were saying, it emerges that you and all the other doctors had constant contact and continuous contact with your patients. Am I right in concluding that from what you said as to the distribution of the rooms and the way in which your department worked; am I right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise for being so long-winded but I wanted to paint a picture for you of our daily contacts and not only daily contacts but if the need -- if a patient had a specific need, then we would see him several times a day, even for brief periods.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in addition to your obligatory daily morning round where you would see each patient individually, you and the rest of the doctors throughout your working hours would be available for contact with patients in view of the organisation of your department; is that right? Can we make that conclusion from your explanations?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that that was how things were organised, and that there were dormitories and then the doctor's room, then another dormitory and then another doctor's room, and so on and so forth, does that mean that, literally speaking, at all times patients would be able to come and find you or you would be able to find a patient?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said that you held separate interviews and conversations with patients in separate rooms without the presence of others. You would have a one-on-one meeting with the patient when you considered that to be necessary. When the young doctors were concerned, like Dr. Simic, for example, would he have separate one-on-one meetings, would you have them, or would you hold these sessions together? Could you explain to us how these sessions took place and how you were mentor to the younger doctor. How would this work?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Official talks which we decurs or take note of after a certain time is done together with the mentor and the young physician together. We have no separate rooms; they were doctor's offices where all the administrative work is conducted, where we have sessions with the patients. They were also the same offices where members of the family would come when they visit in order to receive the necessary information and also for additional work with the family members. We have to give a lot of information to parents and spouses. They ask us a great deal of things, so all this is done in the doctor's room, the doctor's office. And the sessions are recorded in the decursus and the mentor is there and we discuss diagnoses and possible further examination. We have the possibility of carrying out electroencephalography today. We have a computerised tomography system, or rather, a scanner, and we also discuss any changes to therapy or any other procedure which is deemed necessary in the treatment of a patient.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Jevtovic, when the patient is admitted to your department and if it is a patient whom you have not seen before who is coming for treatment, does the doctor take down all the family particulars, that is to say, information about the ancestors, diseases, or anything -- hereditary diseases or anything that could be relevant in the treatment of the patient?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Correct procedure is the following: To collect as much information and data as possible, especially if, as you have just said, we are dealing with a newly-admitted patient. If it is possible to arrive at that information, if there's a family member present accompanying the patient, which is frequently the case, then we research into the patient since his childhood. We look at the key elements, which are possible behavioural difficulties in childhood, during puberty, adolescence, during Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. compulsory military service, and of course, changes in behaviour for which the patient was brought to our department with an insistence upon the way in which their behaviour has changed, the time that this change of behaviour occurred, and possibly treatment, the treatment of the patient before coming to our institution, what treatment the patient had prior to coming to us. A vital piece of information is delving into family anamnesis, family case history, so we always ask whether there were any physical diseases and, most particularly, whether there was any mental diseases in the family. Those are regular questions that we ask. We always ask whether any family member has been treated for a mental illness, whether any family member committed suicide, whether they committed a murder or any other criminal act, whether they were convicted, and whether, generally speaking, in the family, there were members who stood out through their behaviour which stepped outside the norms of normal, regular behaviour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Jevtovic, asking these questions and coming by this type of information and getting the answers, is that the duty and obligation of each doctor treating a patient?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: It is his duty and need. It is a requirement for future work. If we are able to, we try and contact an individual who could give us the information we need. Very often, patients themselves come to us forcibly, they are forced to come. They are brought by a police escort without any family members in attendance, so whether they are brought in from their homes or whether they are brought in because they have been found in some public place where their conduct was inadequate, inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say this, Mrs. Jevtovic, in situations of that kind, are these situations where you are unable to come by the information you need or do you somehow manage to get answers to your basic questions?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: In our service and department, we have a social worker and it is the task of that social worker, when we're talking about that sphere of activity, to see in every way possible if he can contact family members for us to be able to get the necessary information. That does not mean that the social worker amasses that information himself, it means that he invites family members to come to the hospital and to talk to the doctors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That's an explanation regarding the information that you seek to collect from family members. What about the patient himself? Are they the same questions that you put to the patient and is it always possible to do so and is it done?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Heteroanamnesis is a part of our work with the aim of obtaining information for the diagnosis. Another part --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Doctor, just one moment. You don't have to go that slowly. All that we are concerned about is that you don't start to answer the question until you see the typing finish. They are very quick, our court reporters, but they are following the interpreters and the problem arises that the interpreters can't keep up if you come in straight after the answer or if you speak quickly. So you don't have to dictate it, as it were, to somebody who is taking it down in handwriting. You can speak a little bit more quickly than you are now.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Another area of work is this so-called interview. It is a conversation with the patient which involves collecting information and also it includes a clinical examination. Collecting information from the patient, we don't consider to be absolutely valid, especially if we are dealing with a psychotic patient, and that is quite normal, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one more question in this area. Was this the procedure that you instructed the doctors whose mentor you were to apply?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, quite.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Jevtovic, will you please look at an exhibit of ours. It is the case history for Mitar Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown, please, Exhibit P138.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to look at it, Mrs. Jevtovic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, as a neuropsychiatrist in the ward, what do you read from this case history?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: If we go in chronological order --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, I would like to ask you the psychiatric part, leaving out the orthopaedic part - that will be explained by orthopaedists - but only what you see related to psychiatry.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I understand. If we go chronologically, on the 5th of July, because of conspicuous behaviour, a psychiatrist was invited for consultation, which means something was happening with the patient. No consultation was done and we see that, on the 5th of July, "Should be transferred to psychiatry," and the signature is that of Dr. Bogdanovic who at the time was in the situation that I have described; he was working at the neurology department and he did duty for us and the 7th of July is a national holiday in our country. Then the patient was transferred to our ward, Dr. Simic examined him on the 8th, which is a working day, and he found him in this condition as he describes, in this condition of excitation. We can see that the situation changed, it improved; a heteroanamnesis was done from which it can be seen that the changes in behaviour started before his arrival in hospital. According to the wife's statement from the beginning of the war conflicts that, since then, he started drinking more, that he was restless, that he found it difficult to concentrate. Then regarding the decursus, after that, there was an improvement. There is still minor incidents in behaviour but, at the request of the spouse, he was released. The final diagnosis is 298.9, which stands for an acute psychotic disorder. When the general symptoms are established for the diagnosis of a psychotic disorder and there are no specific disorders, so-called psychopathological phenomena which would determine more specifically the type of mental disorder, one could see this as a provisional working diagnosis even though, according to the classification, this diagnosis does exist. It could include certain unspecified alcoholic psychoses because there are unspecific alcoholic psychoses, also reactive psychoses, which were also covered by this code. These are old codes from the former international classification. Nowadays, different codes are in use, and not only the codes have changed but, in some cases, the method of classifying psychiatric diseases has also changed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Maybe I'll come back to that diagnosis a little later because I haven't reached that point yet though we do find it in this case history, you have already started explaining it, but I would like to ask you first when you were talking about the information that is collected from family members and you told us what kind of information is solicited as being relevant, you said that that information is taken note of. Where would that information be recorded in the specific case of this patient if information of that kind had been collected such as that members of the family had been ill or something like that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Exclusively in the case history, but it doesn't mean that every doctor was able to solicit such information. In our population, such facts are concealed relating to suicides and mental disease so it is quite possible that this was covered up. I don't believe that my colleague didn't ask about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if such important matters were raised such as mental diseases of ancestors, parents, or close relatives, or suicides, in the event of a positive answer, then you are telling us that that would necessarily have to have been recorded in the case history?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it would have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please look at the next exhibit, the therapy sheet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could P165 be shown to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you look at the therapy sheet for the treatment of patient Mitar Vasiljevic. Have you looked at the document?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please tell us what you conclude -- what you can conclude from the therapy sheet regarding the therapy administered and whether you can make any conclusions regarding the intensity of the disease of Mr. Vasiljevic on the basis of that therapy sheet.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: From the beginning of treatment on the 7th, 8th, 9th, the patient was having intensive anti-psychotics and neuroleptics. We have not -- we are not familiar with a stronger neuroleptic than Topral and Nozinan has a sedative and anti-psychotic effect. These are the two strongest drugs in use in our country. Unfortunately, we don't have Topral any longer. We had it for a year or two and not since then. Also, we can see that the patient was given injections, which means that he was extremely restless and refused therapy. We avoid vials because neuroleptics are most unpleasant, they have very unpleasant side effects and the reason for such high dosages must exist because it would be absolutely wrong and even criminal to give such strong medicine if they weren't necessary. After a time, he calmed down and he was treated with Largactil tablets, which are milder, but again, 400 milligrams a day is a large dosage. Then he -- the dose was increased to 600 so that, on the 19th, there were problems. This is my handwriting. I must have been on duty. Flormidal is a very strong hypnotic which has a very speedy effect and puts the patient to sleep, so there was a relapse on the 19th and it's quite possible, because he was on tablets, that he omitted to take them, because this happens. They are very clever in concealing a pill. You wouldn't believe what kind of tricks they resort to so that, sometimes, we give the tablets in powder form. We don't have neuroleptics in solutions, which is much more convenient. Then we also see that he was discharged with a considerable dose of Largactil, of 300 milligrams which is, again, quite a considerable dose for treatment at home, so I assume that his situation was not fully resolved, and this is confirmed by the fact that it was at the request of the wife that he was sent home. So this dosage was not quite appropriate for taking at home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Jevtovic, when you're talking about this dose and the therapy administered for home or outpatient treatment, could you be a little more precise? Because you said, "quite a considerable dose," it could mean sufficient or it could mean above average. Was that what you meant to say when you were commenting on his discharge prior to such a decision being made by the doctors?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe I didn't use the best term but I was saying that the strength of the dose is explained by the premature discharge. If a psychotic disorder, which usually is the first treatment, the dosage is too high for outpatient treatment. For an old psychosis that has been treated for a long time, then a patient could be discharged with such a dose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were speaking about the beginning of therapy, and you mentioned Topral as one of the strongest medicines that you had access to in those days, does that mean that that was one of the most effective medicines for such a disease which you resorted to in the treatment of Mitar Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Topral was administered for extremely agitated patients as the strongest neuroleptic that we had at the time, which means that the patient, at the time, was extremely agitated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's as far as Topral is concerned, but generally speaking, when you look at the therapy administered for this period of time, can you tell us how serious the disorder was? Was it average, below average, or above average on the basis of the therapy that he was given?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: From this therapy, we can see that this was an extremely agitated patient and one can also see that this was an unspecified psychosis because there are no other neuroleptics which are more targeted for a particular specific psychosis and there are no antidepressants or something else that are prescribed for other specific psychoses. And this confirms that 298.9 was justified. One could suspect that this was a maniform disorder and one may ask why this was not indicated. A mania, it's an affective disorder which affects the mood and it rarely occurs alone. It is usually combined with depressive states and it could be called mania co-depressive affective disorder. The rule in our work is to wait for at least two such episodes before we can define it as such a psychosis. On the basis of the first psychosis, it is not proper to diagnose it immediately. These are usually younger people who are manifesting such problems early on and having such a fixed diagnosis can harm them in their later life so we need a little Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. time to establish the diagnosis. We can't be hasty upon the first episode and to claim the patient a manic patient, which is a very serious disease and it can cause him great difficulty in later life, so we need time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, Dr. Jevtovic, in this case, this was not registered in the case of Mitar Vasiljevic, no such disorder was established?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: We would not add to the basic diagnosis, especially as the old codes did not allow it. According to the old classification, we didn't have an acute subschizophrenia as a separate disease. There's a separate code for this disease in the new classification which we didn't have before so we were taught not to do that and that was the practice that we applied.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You referred to the first and second episode. What would be the first episode? Would that be a disorder of this kind and a treatment of that patient as one episode? So in the event of a repeated episode, you would make that conclusion? Could you explain that a little?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Acute psychotic disorders need not always develop into a chronic psychosis. It may occur once and never again. But with time, it may develop and become differentiated, and that is why I said the diagnosis of chronic mental disorders have to be followed over time. Though this is a maniform disorder, one needs at least two episodes before being able to qualify this as a manic psychosis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said, Mrs. Jevtovic, that this resembled a maniform disorder, but as it was, the first episode, it was difficult to make such a conclusion and you would like that -- time for that to be confirmed, I understood that part, but I'm asking what was it that resembled a maniform disorder? What were the symptoms pointing in that direction?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: The extreme restlessness of the patient and very conspicuous, uncritical behaviour. Then, also, there is some information here in the decursus about his incoherent speech which says that his thought process was accelerated, accelerated but not contextually disordered thoughts, crazy ideas. There are no deceptions. There are no hallucinations that would lead us in another direction. Also, in the anamnesia by the wife, alcohol was referred to. Alcohol also could be referred to as an etiological factor and have some effect on our conclusion and that's why they opted for an acute psychotic disorder because the code 298.9 in those days included nonspecific alcoholic psychosis, as I said at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Jevtovic, do I take it that what you now found was there were a number of elements of a maniform disorder, but without a fresh verification, a repetition of some situation, you did not wish to take note of such a thing?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: It is not our practice to do that. It doesn't depend on our wish.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the etiological factor, in this case alcohol. How does alcohol or alcoholism affect what you have been telling us about so far?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Such behaviour could lead us to conclude that this was an unspecific alcoholic psychosis because, according to this classification, alcoholic nonspecific psychoses come under this code and their manifestations are similar; general agitation, fear, inconsideration, noncritical behaviour. As for a -- we cannot say that it was specific alcoholic psychosis because they are very characteristic, easily recognisable and no mistake can be made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean "no mistake can be made"? Are you referring to specific alcoholic psychosis?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's an acute, peracute serious alcoholic psychosis known as delirium tremens, and because of vegetative neurosystem disorders, there are specific visual deceptions, hallucinations of tiny animals. These are very specific that do not occur in other mental disorders. They are very typical of delirium tremens. Then there is general bodily tension, fatigue of the whole body, fear, disorientation. The patient sees himself as being in two different places at the same time. This is a very picturesque symptomatology so one can't make a mistake. Then there is alcoholic halluncinosis, which is a specific mental disorder of a more chronic type which again is characterised by numerous hallucinations of the auditive type when the patient is constantly hearing voices, voices that keep telling him off, that threaten him, that speak badly of him and he's fearful, restless, an insomniac, and as a result he cannot behave rationally. He cannot separate reality from his hallucinations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, I think if you ask another question, the answer may take us well into the lunch hour. We'll take the break now and resume again at 2.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Jevtovic, we'll pick up where we left off just before the break. If you remember, we were discussing certain symptoms, that is, we were talking about alcoholic psychosis and delirium tremens. Taking into account the documents that you have and that are in front of you and that you are familiar with, in this particular case of Mitar Vasiljevic, could it have been delirium tremens?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Under no circumstances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please elaborate a little and tell us the reasons why you believe it could not have been delirium tremens.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: In answer to your question before the break, I think I described in detail the symptoms of delirium tremens as a very specific, particular, conspicuous psychosis with a number of physical manifestations, irritability of the vegetative neurosystem reflected in excessive sweating, trembling, redness in the face, and psychologically pronounced restlessness, extreme fear, and numerous hallucinations. Not just any kind of hallucinations but very particular ones, that is, seeing small animals crawling over one's body, and the patient keeps shaking his clothing, shaking them off. Such patients also experience paraesthetic hallucinations coming from the body, as if they have a hair in their mouth. They keep spitting it out. So I think what I've said shows that it is a very specific type of psychosis and that it is not possible to be misled in establishing the diagnosis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From what you have said, I gather, Mrs. Jevtovic, that you are quite certain that in this case of Mitar Vasiljevic it is not delirium tremens.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: It definitely was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From what you have been able to see in the documents, my question is: Do you personally remember Mitar Vasiljevic as a patient?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I do not. It was ten years ago. He was not my patient, he was the patient of a young doctor. I had my own patients. I had a day when I was on duty all day in the outpatient's dispensary as it was July, it is quite possible that I supervised the work of another young doctor or maybe we all took care of all the patients at the same time, I can't remember those details now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Jevtovic, when you were telling us who was working with you among the doctors, I notice you mention another doctor with the same first name as you, Slavica?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Not at the psychiatric ward, at the neuropsychiatric ward. There was a young doctor, Slavica Ivkovic, and she specialised in neurology and so she was automatically attached to the neurological department so that, in 1992, she was not in our ward.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but I am asking you about your own department. So there was no other lady by the name of -- lady doctor by the name of Slavica?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown Exhibit P161, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, will you please look at this exhibit which was found together with the other documents taken by the Prosecution and the Prosecution has tendered it into evidence. So would you please carefully read both pages upon which I can ask you a few questions. Have you looked at both pages on both sides of the paper?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, Madam Jevtovic, do you perhaps recognise this letter? Was that a letter addressed to you and do you have any recollection of that letter?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it rare or frequent for patients to write letters of that kind?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Patients often write to us, either making a request of some sort or expressing their gratitude or sending us a verse of poetry or trying to convince us that they are well and that they should go home, which is the most frequent case, and that they are being held by mistake, so it's no wonder that I don't remember this as it is not at all unusual for patients to write letters. Furthermore, from this letter, one can see that the patient still has problems with his thought process. It is still confused, spread out. The request he makes, and as he addressed me personally, that is -- I assume that it was because, during the rounds, he must have assessed that I was a doctor of some importance, more important than the young doctors, and he hoped he would achieve more through me. Then also, it is absolutely not necessary for anyone to write a letter if they wish to have additional physical examinations. We always ask them, "Are you feeling any pains?" Especially when we have serious patients, we feel that we may neglect physical disease, so we always inquire, and especially if he's taking neuroleptics, a patient may be sleepy, so this request that he makes is quite unnecessary. The second thing that is excessive, which indicates his effective disorder are these threats, as far as I am able to read it - he threatens to go on a hunger strike - that it is quite illogical. People are going for examinations daily, to see the eye doctor, the nose doctor. If he had been in good shape, he would have realised that, but obviously this was written early on in the course of his treatment while he was still not well. Also, this Serb symbol, a symbol of Serbhood, the figures on the letter is just something one doesn't put all over the place, so this also corroborates my opinion that this was a milder hypermanic behaviour, at least, as far as this part of the letter is concerned. The other things that he mentions about the purchase of sweets in a shop, this also shows that he was a bit accelerated, that it was in haste. He ran to the hospital lobby to make that purchase. That must have been when he was in the orthopaedics department because he couldn't have left our department, and in that haste, he incurred a debt. So I have nothing more to say unless you have some more questions for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of the date that you find in two places in this letter, maybe you could look in the therapy sheet to see how that fits in with the therapy because I think the letter was written already in the second stage of his treatment. So would you check that, please, and tell us.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I noticed the date. That was the sixth day after his -- he was transferred to our ward and I have noted that this was in the first stage of his treatment, if it was written on the 13th, that is only after six days. He was transferred on the 7th and this was on the 13th. So by that time, he couldn't have considerably improved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please look at this last sentence before his signature on the second page, where he says, "I would also like to ask you to tie both my hands and legs."

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: This may sound strange, but we hear this sometimes in our department. This maniform disorder that I have described, and his restlessness and -- is very tiring. Imagine as if you were on the move 24 hours a day, it's very tiring. And this happens to many patients. And also among these -- as a result of the medicines, they have a hypnotic effect which can make them drowsy, but it doesn't mean that if somebody is drowsy, he is calm. The neuroleptics have their effect through brain centres, they have a sedative effect and a hypnotic effect. If all these things are not properly adjusted, a person can't fall asleep and sometimes the patients say, "Please tie me up," and that would be my interpretation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you meet such requests of your patients when they want to be tied up, or do you make your own judgement as to whether it is necessary?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we do as they ask because experience tells us that they calm down, and after that, we untie them. Also, we have specially leather collars lined with felt so they don't touch the skin directly. They're wide, they don't cause any damage. So it's not as awful as one might Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. think, at first glance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam Jevtovic, would you please look at the discharge paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I have Exhibit D30.1.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: It's fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that discharge certificate, the same number of the diagnosis can be found, the same code that you spoke about. I think there's also a description. Will you please look at it and see whether there is something additional to what we've seen in the other documents, and then I will ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: The discharge certificate says all that is important taken over from the case history, as far as the psychiatric condition is concerned, only in summary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The condition that you, yourself, described as acute psychosis, the condition Mitar Vasiljevic was in when he was brought to your department, do you find those characteristics here, and could you tell us what precedes that, that is, the period that precedes such a condition, what would be the characteristics of the behaviour of such a person? Is there something that has been medically established regarding conduct of such a person?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: His behaviour, prior to hospitalisation at the psychiatric ward, as far as I can see from the case history, we have the information given by the wife, which were particularly pronounced after he was called in to the Territorial Defence, intensified drinking and changes in behaviour. As far as the orthopaedic department is concerned, the decursus tell us that the problem started on the 5th when consultation was first required. As for the beginning of the psychotic disease, it can start quite suddenly but that is rare. We can have reactive psychoses that start suddenly, and these can start after exposure to very great stress, then also post-natal psychosis, the next day after delivery, because of sudden hormonal changes in the body. We've also said that delirium tremens is acute psychosis which can start suddenly. And these unspecified acute psychoses cannot start so suddenly. Their development can be can be monitored over several weeks and even three or four months sometimes. The problem is that the patient is not constantly drastically changed and that is why relatives don't bring him. They would tell us, you know, "We wanted to bring him in and then he was better the next day," and these things develop gradually. And then psychotic decompensation occurs when reality is completely eliminated when the patient can no longer control himself. We call that acute psychotic decompensation and that is when hospitalisation is essential and that is the condition in which they usually come. If that was your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean, Madam Jevtovic, that in the prior period, there were fluctuations, there were times when you can notice deviant behaviour and there are times when the patient appears to be acting quite normally, like any other person? Am I correctly interpreting your answer?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, quite so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam Jevtovic, you mentioned reactive psychoses. Would you tell us what that is.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Those are psychotic, acute psychotic conditions that occur immediately after exposure to a stressful situation. This is a kind of psychosis that can break out immediately or the very day or the following day after the stressful event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For such a stressful event, a stress of greater proportions is required?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is described as an extremely stressful situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could that be the death of a close relative?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, it could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could it be attending the killing of several persons or the murder of several people and witnessing such an act? Could that be considered a sufficiently stressful situation for a person who never witnessed any such thing before?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I said that reactive psychotic conditions occur quite abruptly, shortly after exposure to stress, but stress can trigger earlier conditions which were about to explode. For example, in alcoholics, people who genetically were prone to act psychotically, then we needed a trigger for the process to be set in motion. Then it wouldn't be reactive psychosis but psychotic reactions when already there was preparation for such reaction, alcoholism or genetic, the genetic factor when younger people develop some hereditary diseases. Psychiatrists acknowledge this as an important etiological factor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of the fact that the condition of acute psychosis that he manifested, one of the symptoms being incomprehensible speech, out of context, is it possible that in the period prior to that period, similar such occurrences may be seen such as illogical speech?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is possible, only milder in intensity and shorter in duration, and so people ignored it without attaching too much importance to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If in such situations there were to be excessive consumption of alcohol, would that increase the possibility?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: All those etiological factors build on one another and increase the intensity of the disorder in the event of excessive alcoholism.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps -- could one say that in such a state, people are prone to exaggerate things, to overestimate one's self and what one is doing? Could that also be a manifestation of this disorder?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: In answer to this question, two possibilities exist or a combination of the two. A pre-morbid personality, which means a person prior to the outbreak of the disease, these things can have an important role. There are people that are histrionic, who attach too much significance to themselves, who expose themselves, who wish to draw attention to themselves, and within the maniform disorder that we have been discussing in his behaviour, this, too, could have an effect. These maniform psychotic patients have intensified reactions, intensified action in everything; they are hyper, they interfere everywhere, they have an opinion on everything, they stand out everywhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Such persons, can they be influenced more easily than others because of this condition of theirs in this particular respect?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Not literally, but the overall situation, if a patient is in the midst of certain extraordinary events or activities, gatherings, he may easily join in even if he is not invited to do so. I don't know if I make myself clear. He has no breaks. He doesn't have sufficient control to set himself limits. He is literally prone to being influenced.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In such a case, if we were talking of some unlawful activity, could we talk about reduced competence because of this condition?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think competence can be assessed in a general way. In order to evaluate competence, very strict rules are required; the time of the act, the type of the act, statements of witnesses, detailed statements, a serious interview with the patient, if he is capable of interpreting his experiences. So the question of competence is not raised in clinical work, these are legal matters and legal categories. It is a highly specific undertaking and I'm afraid you can't assess it just like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I should just like to go back to one point that we discussed but I didn't actually ask you this question. When you spoke about the information that you seek from each patient or family member, and you told us what the important points to focus on are, do you ask for information about previous hospitalisation for some disorder that could be linked to the patient and why he was brought into hospital?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we've already spoken about that. We said that one of the first questions is that we ask him whether he was treated for a mental illness of any kind. In the case history, it was noted that he had been treated for alcoholism.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it necessary to record this and was this checked out in this concrete case, judging on the case history you have before you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Usually we ask for the discharge sheet to have a look at it, and the family members bring this in. If the discharge sheet is lost, then we look for the patient card where a copy of the discharge sheet should exist, and if that is lost, then in the card or file, we see what the general practitioner says, and all instances of hospitalisation have been -- were recorded. But in cases like this one, it was probably unsuccessful, a futile attempt because it was war, it was a period of war; communications were very poor, it was difficult to travel, and between Visegrad and Uzice, there was the front, the war line. And you couldn't cross that line whenever you wanted to unless you had special permits and so on and so forth, so it was war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I am aware of that. But if you were told that in 1984, the patient was treated for alcoholism in your hospital in Uzice twice, would that have been recorded and would you have been able to get at the case history when he came, was admitted to your department, had you had that piece of information, had you known that at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: This information of previous hospitalisation was given to the patient by the patient to his doctor during the first interview, but he said he was hospitalised three times. I said in acute cases, the anamnesis are not -- that you get from a patient is not always valid and so perhaps the doctor didn't look for those case histories precisely because of that. But when the wife came and she was able to confirm that, he was taken home that day, so once again, there was no time to do that. But I have explained several times in explaining the diagnosis that the question of alcoholism was discussed here and that it was one of the factors that made us class this into a nondifferentiated psychosis, which would include an alcoholic nonspecific psychosis as well, alcohol-related.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mrs. Jevtovic, I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Cross-examination, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Groome:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Madam Jevtovic, my name is Dermot Groome and I will be asking you a few questions on behalf of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to clarify a few matters that you discussed in your testimony. You said that you have no specific memory of Mr. Vasiljevic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I take it from that that you don't have any specific memory regarding how much direct contact that you may have had with Mr. Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly, but the principle of my work is to have continuous contact and this is a continuous principle so there is no reason why I shouldn't have the same amount of contacts with him. The number of contacts depends on the type of disorder that the patient is suffering from. Some patients with mental illnesses which lead them to have some ideas, we have crazy ideas we have more need to see them. For us, it was not as interesting that way; we didn't get any contents and substance from him, we just saw that he was very agitated and we had to follow that condition of agitation to see how it would develop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in your testimony you used the word "differential diagnoses." Can you please explain what you mean by "differential diagnoses."

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: To examine the patient clinically, when you draw the conclusion on the basis of heteroanamnesis interview and clinical examination and possibly an additional psychological testing and all the other tests that I mentioned, it is customary that older doctors too should give thought to what the disease could be with all this kind of symptomatology. We use that when we have young doctors in training; we give them food for thought. We can combine these systems and there is no clear-cut form or clear-cut things. Symptoms can be a disruption of physical symptoms but whether he is more affective or whether his personality is disintegrated , or his system of thinking, there's a dilemma; you have to weigh it all up. And there is a group of psychoses which are called schizophrenic psychoses, for example, or paranoid schizophrenic psychoses. It can lead us astray to begin with. We might think it's paranoid psychosis, pure paranoid psychosis because the symptoms are at the same, particularly in the beginning at the initial stages, so that too is a subject for discussion and differential diagnostics, as we call it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now you've touched upon, in that last answer, about a clinical examination, and there were a few questions I wanted to ask you about that. Given that you were supervising young doctors at the time, was there a standard battery or protocol of tests or steps that you expected the doctors working under you to take when they conducted a clinical examination of a new patient on your ward?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: To conduct a psychiatric examination, that is standardised. There are methods to test each psychological function and each psychological Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. function must be recorded. The examination begins with the description of the patient's appearance. Young doctors are taught that patients must be looked at clinically even before he comes to the department, for example. If he has been brought in handcuffed, for example, if he has come in dirty, unkempt, if he is without shoes and it's winter. All that is -- demands our full attention because it is the way we assess and appraise the condition of the patient, so this entire protocol of examination must be recorded and we must see that a young doctor has looked into all this. There is a small intelligence test as well and the clinician is duty-bound to apply this IQ because intellectual testing is done by psychologists because they have international tests, but our clinical appraisal includes that too. So -- and then we have standardised questionnaires, for example, for certain symptoms of a disease. For depression, for example, there are several tests for depression. One of them is Hamilton's scale for depression where this is expressed numerically, and you can look at Hamilton's scale, you can see the degree of depressiveness. So if two scales coincide with a high coefficient of depressiveness, that means that that psychopathological disorder is a depressive one. Then you have one for fear, for anxiety. There are lots and lots of tests to determine anxiety. So there is the possibility of objectivising a young doctor's work. I don't have to stand over him all the time, he brings it to me or we go through it verbally, orally, because you have seen the number of doctors that were working in the hospital at the time. I know the importance of documents. I go to court and a nice case history is an enormous help to me but, quite honestly, under the circumstances in those conditions, it was not always possible to do these things, which doesn't mean that we didn't discuss them orally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you've mentioned at least four tests just now; appearance, a test for intelligence, certain questions such as the Hamilton's scale, and certain queries made for the level of anxiety. Are there other tests that you would expect a doctor working under you to check into when they do a clinical examination of a new patient? And if you could just list them and I will maybe ask you to explain a few of them afterwards.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I mentioned that there is an order in which we test psychological functions and that is a type of psychiatric examination that you learn at school; verbal contact, his appearance, his thinking, his affective response, intelligence. It is all standard. Critic -- his able -- his ability to have a critical appraisal and so on, so that is what the young doctor reports to me on. Not all these functions need be impaired but we have to take them in their order to see where the prevalent disturbance and disorder occurs and then we'll move in that direction and sound out the patient further.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that, in order for you to properly supervise a patient - for example, to decide that a suggested therapy is the proper one - that you really need to have this assessment done and presented to you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Of course, but I have daily insight into the therapy, how far the therapy is being tolerated. Those are things that we can do externally. We can't determine the level of neuroleptics in the blood, for example. In developed countries, this is done, but it is a laboratory experimental finding but not used in daily practice. There is only one neuroleptic whose level we set on a daily basis and that is Lithium, and we do that regularly, in the frequency that is necessary and depending how long the patient has taken these neuroleptics, but externally, through the clinical impression, how much he has been sedated, how much his condition has improved, how somnolent he is. I said that neuroleptics, earlier on, or anti-psychotics are very unpleasant for the patient, they have unpleasant effects on certain parts of the brain and, therefore, create side effects or neuroleptic syndromes which are visible. The patient has enormous salivation, he is rigid, his face appears rigid, he can have very unpleasant contraction of the muscles, muscular contraction, and his spine might contract, very bizarre positions and poses which are painful, so you can see all this, can you observe it in a patient.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, you said the patient was seen on the daily rounds and you said that three people see the patient; the head nurse, the psychologist, and the working therapist. Could I ask you; Dr. Simic, was he the psychologist or the working therapist in this case?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Simic was a young doctor who was being trained from the beginning. Our young doctors are employed in a targeted fashion, he is educated in one stream, but it takes a long time for the ministry of health to authorise a specialist training for a doctor and to wait for this status to be authorised, he is what we call a secondary doctor but doing practically the same work so we know that he is going to be one of our doctors ultimately, we don't wait for him to receive authorisation, he starts this process straight away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, let me ask you; who would have been the psychologist who would have seen Mr. Vasiljevic on a daily round? Who would that person have been?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: In our service, we have two psychologists who have graduated from the faculty of psychology. They do psychological testing, diagnostics, psycho-social support for the family and they are regularly employed in the department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell from the records before you which -- what was the name of the psychologist who saw Mr. Vasiljevic on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: With an acute psychotic disorder, that has nothing to do with the psychologist. Psychologist uses healthy parts of a personality to pull the patient out of his disorder. Acute psychosis, acute psychotic processes excludes patients from reality as a whole so that, for that domain, for that type of illness, a psychologist is no good to you. It is only when the condition is improved and when a patient's condition has improved, can we go on to do psychological testing to assess personality to see how far we have come in our treatment, although that is clinical. The psychologist has quite a different role to play.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the working therapist, who can you tell us what would be the name of the working therapist that would have seen Mr. Vasiljevic on the daily round?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: A working therapist visits the patients to get to know them and for the patients to get to know the technicians so that when he starts his working therapy it is not somebody they don't know, but they don't go to working therapy straight away. A person goes to attend working therapy when the therapist believes that he has the patience to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Doctor, please, let's just answer the question. If you know, say so. If you don't know, say so. You weren't asked to describe what happened. What was the therapist?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a working therapist working with Mr. Vasiljevic, if you know?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you talked about, in addition to the daily rounds, that there being a -- I think you described them as being official talks in the doctor's office, and you described this as the place where some of the most sensitive material or subject matter was discussed with a patient; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, would the occurrence of such an office visit or office talk, would that be recorded in the medical history somewhere?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: They are recorded if they are substantive. We mentioned the disorders where there are massive ideas, crazy ideas, hallucinations and so on, but this is a psychosis which was manifest only in agitation. He didn't have anything to tell the doctor. He just demonstrated his agitation and restlessness, his acceleration, his hyper mood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, from the fact that there are no such official talks or visits to the doctor's office recorded here, can we conclude from that that either Mr. Vasiljevic had no talks within the doctor's office or, as you suggest now, there was nothing substantive that was discussed in those visits?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: We have a decursus morbi on the 8th of July and the 15th of July and also on the 28th of July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would that indicate that on those two dates there had been office visits that -- your office visits that you described?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: May I read you the decursus of the 15th of July?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Actually, Doctor, that's in evidence, and we've heard it many times now. If you would just answer my question. Does that indicate to you that -- that note there, does it indicate to you that there was this visit or this discussion with Mr. Vasiljevic inside the doctor's office?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: The decursus shows this because the doctor describes his manner of speech. The doctor describes his conduct and way of talking. This is done on the 15th of July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, I want to ask you to just clarify what you said in response to a question by Mr. Domazet. I believe you stated that the last line in that letter from Mr. Vasiljevic to you that's P161, the last letter where Mr. Vasiljevic requests to be tied up, you said that such a request could quite possibly be the result of the medications that he was on; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Not the medication, the basic disorder, the basic disorder, that is, that therapy had not still reached its goal of recovery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you had mentioned, I believe, that these neuroleptics have a number of side effects and one of them was this amount of hyperactivity; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Not hyperactivity. Hyperactivity is a symptom of the disease. The neuroleptic syndrome is with muscular rigidity, salivation. And due to the muscular rigidity, the patient assumes bizarre positions, and his body is constricted when the paravertebral muscles are constricted and it is very painful but we deal with this symptom with additional therapy. According to this therapy, Vasiljevic did not have neuroleptic disturbances. Had he had them, he would have been given Artan or Procipar which deal with that. We can't work without neuroleptics, of course, but there are medicines which can deal with these side effects. And if we see that the patient is in a bad condition, we give him an intravenous drip, deal with that situation, make a small pause, and then go ahead and continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, let me ask you about the delirium tremens. I believe what you've told us is that the symptoms of delirium tremens are very obvious symptoms; is that correct? There's no need to repeat them all but just that they are very obvious symptoms; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, completely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would I be correct in thinking that any trained doctor, not a -- a doctor wouldn't have to necessarily be a neuropsychiatrist to recognise them? Any competent doctor would recognise the symptoms of delirium tremens; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Well, my experience tells me that not every doctor would. Very frequently, they call abstinence delirium tremens, ordinary abstinence, and every kind of restlessness, inadequate, inappropriate behaviour. They tend to use the term loosely and say he's entered into a delirium. And we see that there are no signs of delirium and then seek another explanation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the word "delirium" sometimes used as an abbreviated way of saying "delirium tremens," as I believe you just did in your last answer? Is that a common way to use the word "delirium," as an abbreviation for "delirium tremens"?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: No, "delirium tremens" is a set category, and "delirium" itself, on its own, is the state of disturbance in the conscious, disturbance of orientation, which is disturbance and disorder of consciousness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it possible that somebody on sedatives, that the sedatives would mask the symptoms of the delirium tremens?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: They can mask them if they are administered in high doses and can even -- it is treated not with neuroleptics but with other types of benzidines, zepin [phoen], epinephrine, other types of drugs. Rarely neuroleptics. And if you have to, then for very brief periods of time. There is a specific haloperidol anti-psychotic which affects the hallucinations. It attacks the hallucination syndrome. So only in that case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, can I draw your attention to the case history, P138, and the note from the 5th of July from Dr. Stojkovic. And the portion of the note that I'm interested in discussing with you is the portion where Dr. Stojkovic says: "The patient shows signs of a stage preceding delirium. He has not been taking the prescribed sedatives for days." In that context, is it possible that what Dr. Stojkovic is describing is his observation of Mr. Vasiljevic entering into the delirium Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. tremens?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: There is the precise qualification here that I said pre-deliriant state. It doesn't say "deliriant," it says "pre-deliriant," which means changes in a behaviour which they were not able to qualify, which was, in fact, this psychosis, agitation, restlessness, uncontrolled behaviour, disobedience. But "pre-deliriant" means nothing. He is either deliriant or he isn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were asked a number of questions regarding reactive psychoses, and you've stated that that could start suddenly immediately after a high-stress situation; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And one of the examples that was used was that if somebody had witnessed a number of people being killed, that be a precipitating event for reactive psychoses; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: It could unleash that, yes, precipitate it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, isn't it equally possible that it could be precipitated -- such a reactive psychoses could be precipitated, let's say in the case of a man who, getting very drunk and upset, killed members of his family. Couldn't that be the kind of situation that when he sobers up and confronts having done that act, couldn't that be a precipitating event for reactive psychoses?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: We said that the effects of alcohol on the mental functioning, especially of individuals who have a certain predisposition in the central nervous system towards that type of reaction which had it not been for that alcohol, would never have entered into a state of psychosis. And as far as your question is concerned, including reactions to a stress situation, I don't think I quite understood you, the last portion of what you said. I'm not quite clear on that.
