utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise. I think I complicated it with the alcohol. Let's just say that a man becomes enraged, kills his wife, and when he calms down and realises the terrible thing he did, could that not be the kind of high-stress incident that could push that man into having reactive psychoses?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: The newspapers are full of such cases. Do you know how many drunken husbands kill their wives, in our country, or in-laws, and then sometimes take their own lives as a result too? Alcohol sets into motion the worst in human beings. If there is a predisposition, either in the structure of the personality or some genetic predisposition, then alcohol is the drop that tips the scale, and if he is aggressive and an explosive personality, then that will be one more superimposed element.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So would you agree with me that an overpowering sense of guilt of having done something very horrible would be something that could precipitate somebody's decline into psychoses?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: He would enter into a state of depressive psychosis. The feeling of guilt and depression go hand in hand. The feeling of guilt is a symptom of depression, one of the symptoms of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if a patient in the past has suffered a psychiatric or -- a psychiatric event or had psychiatric problems every time he has previously withdrawn from alcohol, is it possible for him to withdraw from alcohol and not have a similar psychiatric event?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: There is less possibility that it is recurrent, but the possibility exists. If he abstains from alcohol, the possibility of that happening is lower.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Domazet asked you a few questions regarding competence and my question to you is, you said that, in order to make a determination on competence, you would need a very thorough interview of the person who was charged with the crime as well as know, in great detail, the circumstances surrounding the crime; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One of the questions you would ask -- or would you explore the person's state of mind or their own assessment of their state of mind at the time of the crime; is that one of the areas that you would explore?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: The difference is in the validity of the statements of the perpetrators immediately after the act he committed and much later, on the condition that he has treated and has recovered and that he is capable of providing valid information and interpreting the event properly that is what it was that spurred him on to commit the act because his statement immediately after is one thing. I know a drastic case. A young man cut up his girlfriend because she had poisoned herself with food. The whole procedure was respected. Many years later, he was treated regularly. He had a far more critical attitude towards it because he disassociated himself from that because he realised that he was sick, and in paranoid psychosis, this can be achieved through treatment because they are not deteriorated intellectually, the personality is not disintegrated to the same extent as in schizophrenia and, after prolonged therapy, they are able to interpret what they thought then, what they felt and what they did, if it is successful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to put to you a question and answer, a question put to Mr. Vasiljevic and an answer that he gave. And so you have some understanding of when this question was asked of him, it was asked about a year ago under a time that we're not aware he was suffering any type of psychological disorder. And then I want to ask you a question afterwards. The question was:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. What I am interested now is at the time of the incident by the river, was your mental state -- were you having any kind of mental problems or psychiatric problems at that time? The answer Mr. Vasiljevic gave was: No, I had problems after that incident, especially since a colleague of mine was killed there. Now, how much weight can we put on Mr. Vasiljevic's own assessment that he was not suffering a psychological disorder at the time of this incident which occurred at a river and it was a crime, that was a reference to a crime? How much weight can we put on his own assessment that he was not suffering from a psychological disorder?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I would be able to give you a more correct answer if at the time he gave you that statement he was examined by a psychiatrist who would be able to assess his condition at the time and the validity of his statement at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we don't have that information. All I can provide you with is that we were not aware of any psychological disorder at that time. Can I ask you: Are you able to tell us how much weight we can put in this statement, assuming that there were no obvious manifestations of a psychological disorder present at the time he made that statement?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: It depends who said that there were no manifestations of disease. I have to know a lot in order to be able to judge somebody's competence and degree of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, let me ask you, for the purposes of this question, if you would assume that there was no psychological disorder present at the time the statement was made. Can I ask you to make that assumption and then tell us can we not put some weight in his own assessment that, at the time of a crime, he was not suffering from a psychological disorder?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: These are highly hypothetical statements. On that basis, it is not possible to make any conclusions about somebody's mental condition and especially not on the degree of his competence. I am very sorry but I am unable to make -- give you an opinion on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Re-examined by Mr. Domazet:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understood well Mr. Groome's question on page 90, row 14, it appears that Mitar Vasiljevic, when asked about his mental state at the time of the incident by the river, said that, at the time, he wasn't having any problems but that, after that, he did, "Because a colleague of mine was killed," it says. And as we're referring to that incident, is it possible if he was present at such an event when, before his very eyes, among others, a colleague of his is executed and, as he said, a good friend of his, would that be the kind of situation that could trigger this reactive psychosis?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I have said several times all the things that can provoke a reactive psychosis; various extremely stressful situations, especially if there is a predisposition on the part of the nervous system to react in this way. And we already have one element, that is alcoholism, which could have contributed to his instability as a personality and to find it difficult to accept loss and exposure to stress.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In answer to a question from Mr. Groome about the daily rounds by doctors of all patients, I think it wasn't quite clear in what you said who made those rounds because it follows from Mr. Groome's statement that, in addition to the head nurse, there was a psychologist and a social worker, and indeed that is what you said. But to make things quite clear for me and all of us, could you please repeat who were all the people who made the morning rounds of patients?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Specialist doctors, young doctors in training, the head of the department when that was planned, the main psychologist, and a work therapist if we had one. These are persons who regularly attend the morning rounds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in addition to the psychologist and possibly this work therapist, all the doctors with the exception of the head of department.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you make your rounds from one patient to another?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, literally so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in that case, it doesn't matter whether a patient needs a psychologist, a work therapist, or whatever?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I have said that the team makes these rounds according to needs. The work therapist goes to meet the patient so that when he goes for work therapy, he will know him. Then also, the therapy sheets are checked and therapy prescribed for that day. We carry them with us, they're not on the beds, for understandable reasons; so that the patient shouldn't scribble anything on them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of your round, do you already agree on therapy or do you not do that in front of the patient but later?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: The therapy is written down on the sheet immediately. The assessments are made on the basis of the reports of the second and third shifts and the doctor on duty the previous day. We have to hear what happened to the patient from the time we left at 1.00 p.m. until the next day in the morning, and what other therapy he was given, and then in the morning, we prescribe the therapy for that day. This need not be the same therapy throughout the day, it may change in the course of the day. We don't have discussions in front of the patient, but we fill in those therapy sheets and there is a special folder for each room and we hand it over to the main nurse and she passes it on to the nurses, who administer the therapy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In answer to a question from Mr. Groome as to whether the work therapist had worked with Mitar Vasiljevic, you said no. My question is: How do you know that and why there was no work therapy. Was there some reason?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't have time to give the Prosecutor a full answer. At the time, we didn't have a work therapist, we got one much later in 1994, maybe 1995, and this was 1992. But even if we had, Mitar Vasiljevic could not have gone to work therapy. He was not in a condition to attend work therapy during his hospitalisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Jevtovic, very much for coming to give evidence and for the evidence which you have given. You are now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we're waiting for the next witness, after examining the ledgers, the Prosecution will only be seeking to have the pages that were in the initial application D26 analysed by a document examiner, so I just wanted to update the Court on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: What about the other books?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The other books, we will not be seeking to conduct examinations on. And with respect to the expert report filed yesterday on the legal expertise, the Prosecution will not be seeking to cross-examine that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, we'll need to get those books back so that somebody down in the registry can start photocopying Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. them. Well, we will not need the original books now other than D26; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Domazet, maybe if you nominate which pages of the other two books you want copied, the books themselves can go home, back to Uzice, and only D26 will need to be kept and that's the one you've already copied, isn't it, D26?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, perhaps I wasn't clear. Although I'm not seeking to have these books examined by a document examiner, there is some important information that I think will be relevant in the Court's determination of these issues so I would ask that, to the conclusion of the trial, that they do be kept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right, well, then that makes it clear. We'll have to get a copy made so that it can go back to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Doctor, will you now make the solemn declaration that is in the document that the usher is showing you there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sit down, please. Yes, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Mr. Domazet:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jovanovic, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Ivan Jovanovic
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, on behalf of the Defence, I will be examining you today and asking you some questions. Please answer my questions but after waiting for a few moments, and also, you can follow on the monitor when the court reporters have completed the transcription since we speak the same language and it is more difficult for the interpreters to keep up with us. Dr. Jovanovic, will you please introduce yourself; tell us your first and last name, the date and place of birth and where you are living today.

utterances.speaker: Ivan Jovanovic
utterances.text: My name is Ivan Jovanovic. I am 40 years old. I was born in Arilje, where I still live, and I am working at the general hospital in Uzice. I've been working there since 1989.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are working in which department of the general hospital at Uzice?

utterances.speaker: Ivan Jovanovic
utterances.text: Since the 23rd of January, 1989, I have been working at the orthopaedics and traumatology department of the general hospital in Uzice. And I was granted a specialisation course in that hospital on the 12th of April and I completed those studies on the 12th of October, 1994. And since then, I have been working independently as an orthopaedic surgeon, a specialist for traumatology and orthopaedic surgery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All this time, Mr. Jovanovic, as you have told us, you have spent at the orthopaedics department of the hospital in Uzice; did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: Ivan Jovanovic
utterances.text: The only interruption I had from September 1992 until 1994 because I had to do part of my specialisation course in Belgrade. Also, from June 1995, for six months I was in the United States and those are the only interruptions that I have had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, I am particularly interested in the period when you were working in 1992. And you told us that you were working in the orthopaedics ward until September of that year; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Ivan Jovanovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to try and look back to that period and the period immediately preceding and after it and tell us, if you can, in those days, that is, sometime in mid-1992, what post you held and who was working with you in the department.

utterances.speaker: Ivan Jovanovic
utterances.text: At that time, I had the status of a doctor on specialist training. With me at the department in the same status was Nada Gordic, Dr. Miroslav Jevtic, and already specialists, as qualified specialists, Dr. Stanisavljevic; Dr. Milosavljevic, who is now retired; Dr. Jovicevic; Dr. Stojkovic; Dr. Moljevic; and Dr. Stojanovic. He left the hospital around about then, so I'm not quite sure whether he was there that very month or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember anything in particular concerning that period as compared to any other period? Was something different in this period of time that I asked you about?

utterances.speaker: Ivan Jovanovic
utterances.text: The period was characterised by a great deal of work that we had primarily because of wartime traumas, and as a department, we were overcrowded. There was a very large influx of patients. I think that was the most characteristic trait of that period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said, Mr. Jovanovic, that one of the characteristics of the period, in addition to a large number of patients, was the state of war, what state of war are you referring to or, rather, where was such a state of war in existence?

utterances.speaker: Ivan Jovanovic
utterances.text: When I say that, I mean exclusively the situation in Bosnia, the events on the left bank of the Drina River from which the injured arrived whom we called the injured from the war zone, loosely speaking, without entering into the details as to how those injuries occurred.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember, Dr. Jovanovic, whether you had the wounded or patients coming from that area of Bosnia and Herzegovina belonging to both ethnic groups, that's Serbs and Muslims, or only one ethnic group? Can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: Ivan Jovanovic
utterances.text: I remember in particular the atmosphere that prevailed during those days, months, and weeks. I remember the atmosphere more than I do faces and names. I remember, and I remember the specific nature of war injuries. And this is unique for one's experience. In my field, you couldn't get such experience anywhere else. So in answer to your question, I remember very well that at first, we had patients belonging to all the ethnic groups, I mean both Christians and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of the fact that a few years prior to that you had started working, Dr. Jovanovic, do you remember that in the period prior to the state of war, as you described it, did you, in those days, also have patients coming from that part of Eastern Bosnia who came to Uzice for hospitalisation or treatment as outpatients? Was this commonplace in the previous period as well?

utterances.speaker: Ivan Jovanovic
utterances.text: The hospital I work in is a regional hospital in Yugoslavia. It covers 500.000 patients, of which 150.000 are from the border area of Bosnia, and it was quite customary before the events in Bosnia, during the events, and even today. And let me add in passing that to this day I have quite a number of patients that I have operated on who are of Muslim faith, and three of them are waiting for me to return from The Hague to be operated. I specialise in, or, rather, my greatest interest is in hip replacement, and at least a third of those patients are of Muslim faith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It's time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Doctor, but we have to adjourn now. We will resume again at 9.30 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: at 4.00 p.m., to be reconvened on Friday the 30th day of November, 2001, at 9.30 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25
